PRIORITIES RESOLUTION

Preamble

DSA meets at its fall 2003 national convention at a time of right-wing dominance in United States domestic and foreign policy. The Bush administration’s doctrine of “pre-emptive” wars involves unilateral United States intervention around the globe in an arrogant and violent manner not witnessed since the Vietnam War and the covert/proxy wars of the 70’s and 80’s. In addition, Bush’s tax give-away to the rich and radical expansion of military spending has created a structural deficit that will place downward pressure on public spending for generations to come. The Bush administration has cynically used the ‘war on terrorism’ to justify an assault on already weakened civil rights and civil liberties, and to justify a massive increase in military spending and a gutting of funding for even its own public policy initiatives, such as “The Global War on AIDS” and “The Leave No Child Behind” educational act. There is no doubt that this is the most reactionary administration in at least a century, especially given its control of all three branches of government. Moreover right wing administrations are less constrained and more vicious during a second term than in their first since they no longer have to be concerned with reelection.

The danger posed by a second term is real. A re-election of the rogue Bush regime would further a unilateral foreign policy that threatens global peace and threaten the destruction of our already minimalist public sector, particularly Medicare, Social Security, and public education. But, the reelection of this President is not certain. There is wide spread popular concern about the economy and foreign policy that has surfaced in the polls and is evident in the strength of the anti-war candidates for the Democratic nomination. The Bush administration’s foreign policy overreach has given rise to a quagmire in Iraq and its failure to aid state budgets has accentuated the costs of the economic downturn. The uneven economic ‘recovery’ has benefited only the affluent, while placing tremendous social welfare burdens on state and local governments.

Thus, the challenge facing the broad democratic left – which includes DSA – is to defeat the Bush administration in the 2004 elections, while also strengthening a coalition of progressive forces that would pressure whatever administration that replaces the Bush regime to implement more humane and democratic foreign and domestic policies. We have no illusion about the centrist character of most of the feasible alternatives to Bush; but politicians necessarily respond to popular pressure from below. How many social gains can be derived from Bush’s defeat will depend on how much the labor, civil rights, environmental, and feminist movements strengthen themselves through this popular resistance to Bush. As socialists, our participation in an anti-Bush campaign will not be simply as builders of someone else’s election. We will proceed with an eye to promoting campaign strategies that can help grow the many social movements we support.

The outcome of the 2004 elections will be the single biggest factor determining the shape of political work in the near future, but regardless of the outcome, we commit ourselves to continue our challenge to America’s low-wage economy and its structural underpinnings.

In engaging in the political and organizational priorities, this convention reiterates the 2001 convention’s commitment that all of DSA’s politics will be guided by a demand for social and economic justice for all. In pursuit of justice, multi-racial coalition building and an anti-racist politics must be an ongoing, integral part of all our projects and activism. We must also consistently look for opportunities to work side-by-side with activists in communities of color.

To move forward towards the goals mentioned above, DSA adopts the following four main priorities at this convention:

I. To participate actively in a Dump Bush movement. This includes :

1) encouraging DSA members to participate actively in the primary campaign of the candidate of their choice;

2) organizing DSA members who are delegates to the convention, providing testimony at platform hearings on our issues, organizing DSA events at the Democratic National Convention and elsewhere, and working to unify the efforts of progressive delegates at the convention;

3) building a sufficiently strong left coalition that it can pressure the campaign to engage in genuine grass-roots mobilizations and put heat on any new administration to adopt the most progressive policies possible.

II. To strengthen DSA’s organizational capacities. DSA must engage in more internal and public education as to the relevance of democratic socialist vision and program for building a more humane world as an alternative to capitalism in the twenty-first century. In particular, the organization must reinvigorate its tradition of educating young people to this politics, particularly – but not exclusively – by rebuilding a DSA/YDS presence on college and university campuses.

III. We must build upon the increased organizational focus and coordinated activism that the “Low Wage Justice” campaign, initiated at the 2001 DSA convention, has brought to the organization. The DSA NPC and national office will continue to provide resources and information to aid locals in living wage campaigns, immigrant justice activism, single payer advocacy, and labor support work.

The national leadership and staff will also work to bring together religious, labor, student, environmental and community activists to build a national campaign to achieve justice for Wal-Mart workers as well as reforms in Wal-Mart’s business practices. We cannot envision victory in our efforts against the low-wage economy without achieving significant and lasting change at Wal-Mart.

IV. With our international connections we will work to develop a project around a public dialogue between progressive elected officials in the United States and other countries. The dialogue would attempt to develop several points.

1) The importance of a genuine multilateral approach to international crises and the need for international leadership on human rights and peace issues from outside the United States.

2) Opposition to American jingoism, anti-Europe bashing, simplistic unilateralist or phony multilateral foreign policy programs, and contempt for international law. Educating the public as to the superior structure of the economic and social welfare systems of other advanced industrial nations.

3) International solidarity to meet human needs and further popular aspirations while opposing corporate-driven globalization.

This convention commits the national staff and NPC to :

Strengthening the relationship between YDS and DSA

The locals and the national will endeavor to provide whatever aid will help YDS re-establish a presence on college campuses (and high schools) around the nation.

Improving the effectiveness of our communication and outreach

We must continue to improve the editorial quality and timeliness of Democratic Left, the DSA web site, and the organization’s listserve.

Regular coverage of local activities shall continue to be part of the mission of Democratic Left and the website.

We must continue to implement the 2001 Convention Resolution on Internet Enabling DSA, including providing an internet discussion list and making minutes available. We should routinely collect email addresses.

In order to expand the pool of members, activists, and contributors (and thus increase our staff and resource capacity), DSA will attempt to return to its practice of mailing 50-100,000 pieces of direct mail recruitment letters each year.

Conferences

This convention also endorses continuing the practice of substituting regional activist conferences for a single, non-convention-year, national activist conference.

Regional conferences and National Conventions should devote more time to democratic discussion and decision-making.

Development Committees

To enhance the relationship between the national office and leadership and our local activists, the NPC will appoint a Local Development Committee consisting of NPC and non-NPC members. This committee will maintain regular communication between locals and organizing committees and the national organization; revise and update a Local Development Plan and work on carrying it out; make recommendations to the national organization in the interest of the health of locals; stimulate discussion about the concerns expressed by locals and the regional activist conferences; and research best practices of DSA locals and how they might learn to do better, and disseminate this information.

Similarly, the NPC will, if possible, appoint an At-Large Development Committee concerned with at-large members.

RESOLUTION ON THE OCCUPATION OF IRAQ

The prosecution of the War in Iraq and the subsequent occupation of Iraq completely validate the objections raised by those who opposed this war. Only the speedy restoration of Iraqi sovereignty to an independent and legitimate Iraqi government can end this quagmire.

To facilitate this, Democratic Socialists of America calls for the immediate withdrawal of the U.S.-British “coalition” forces from Iraq and simultaneous transfer of administration of Iraq to the United Nations, including the appointment of a UN High Commissioner. A UN-controlled peacekeeping force should maintain security during the period of UN administration while an Iraqi force is being developed and sovereignty is restored.

The Bush administration has failed to provide for even the most minimal needs of the Iraqi population. While corporations such as Halliburton and Bechtel are profiteering from no-bid contracts, U.S. citizens are paying for an old-fashioned colonial occupation in which U.S. troops—assigned to state-building duties for which they have no training—are being routinely killed. Iraqi civilians, too, are being killed in armed attacks by U.S. soldiers, by insurgents, and by common criminals taking advantage of the breakdown in social order. The Iraqi people are also suffering and dying due to their lack of sufficient clean water, electricity, and medical care. Its infrastructure destroyed, Iraq is being ravaged, and ethno-nationalist and reactionary Islamist forces are on the rise. DSA condemns the wholesale privatization of the Iraqi economy carried out unilaterally by the U.S. occupying forces. Only a sovereign and democratic Iraqi government can implement legitimate structural and economic reforms. DSA supports the efforts of organizations such as U.S. Labor Against the War that seek to protect workers’ rights and support an independent trade union movement in Iraq.

The Bush administration called for the creation of a UN-endorsed multilateral military force to join the U.S. occupation force in Iraq, to be commanded by an American and accountable to the Pentagon’s strategic control. As Phyllis Bennis of the Institute for Policy Studies noted, the plan did “not envision Washington even sharing authority and decision-making with the UN itself or with the governments sending international contingents, let alone ending its occupation and turning over full authority to the UN to oversee a rapid return to Iraqi independence.” We reject the administration’s arrogance.

We further demand that the U.S. and British meet their moral and legal responsibilities under international law by providing for the humanitarian costs of their unilateral intervention. Washington and London must pay the continuing costs of Iraq's reconstruction, including much of the cost of UN humanitarian and peacekeeping deployments. The Bush administration must immediately make public a realistic estimate for the cost of reconstruction in Iraq and turn over funds to UN authority, beginning with the $87 billion dollars allegedly appropriated for reconstruction (but the majority of which is aimed at supporting the military costs of United States occupation). Reconstruction funds would be far cheaper than the costs incurred by continuing the inhumane and counter-productive United States unilateral occupation of Iraq.

RESOLUTIONS ON ELECTORAL POLITICS

RESOLUTION REGARDING DSA ORGANIZING AROUND THE DEMOCRATIC NATIONAL CONVENTION

Whereas the Democratic Party will be holding it's 2004 Presidential nominating convention in Boston, and,

Whereas we as socialists seek to support our allies in the labor, racial and ethnic minority, feminist and peace movements within the Democratic Party, and,

Whereas it is important that socialists seek to influence the debate within the Democratic Party and articulate a democratic socialist vision for American politics, and,

Whereas it is vital that Democratic Socialists of America increase it's visibility and provide public forums for socialist ideas, and,

Whereas the Boston local is one of the largest local organizations in DSA,

Therefore be it resolved that the national organization of DSA and the Boston local shall jointly organize a public socialist event at or concurrent with the Democratic Party’s national convention in Boston in July of 2004.

RESOLUTION ON POLITICS

WHEREAS, DSA does not automatically assume that a Democratic President, even with a Democratic House and Senate, or any lesser Democratic officeholder at any level, will automatically be a progressive, or move in a progressive direction;

THEREFORE, be it resolved that DSA recognizes that left pressure will still need to be applied when Democrats are elected or re-elected at any level; and

THEREFORE, DSA will actively work to apply such pressure through itself and through left and progressive coalitions, at the national, state and local level, through all agencies available – progressive and grassroots organizations, trade unions and Jobs with Justice chapters, organizations of women and minorities, educational forums, and, just as important, through demonstrations and protests in the streets.

RESOLUTION ON ELECTORAL REFORM

DSA reaffirms its support for constitutional and electoral reforms to create a more democratic and representative political system in the United States, including:

Public funding for electoral campaigns.

Equitable access of candidates to mass media and the elimination of privately purchased campaign ads.

Limits on the size of individual campaign contributions and on total campaign spending.

The abolition of corporate PACs.

Same-day voter registration, and 24-hour voting on weekends or a national holiday for Election Day.

The elimination of the undemocratic Electoral College.

Experiments with proportional representation, electoral “fusion," and single-transferable ballot and "instant runoff" voting, so that people may vote for what they believe in without fearing that their votes will be wasted.

Equitable financing and provision of crucial public goods: not only standardized, high-quality machinery but also a voter-verifiable permanent audit trail. Any voting technology should allow preferential voting, including instant runoff and proportional representation.

Restoration of full voting rights to convicted felons.

DSA supports efforts to defend the right to vote, and we condemn the racist programs of the Republican Party and others to deny ballot access to minority voters, such as in Florida in 2000.

RESOLUTION ON MISSION STATEMENT

The NPC shall initiate an organization-wide discussion aimed at the development of a mission statement. Until such time as wider discussions within the organization – including at the planned regional activist conferences – may result in a better formulation, the following shall serve as DSA’s working mission statement:

Democratic socialists fight for a world in which all people participate democratically in the governing of the economic, political and cultural institutions and relationships that shape their lives. In the near term, this means that democratic socialists struggle for reforms that shift power and resources away from corporate elites and put them in the hands of ordinary people. The mission of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is to participate in establishing democratic socialism as a political force in the United States and the world by training and mobilizing socialist activists; by educating the public about the democratic socialist values of equality, liberty and solidarity; and by helping to build progressive coalitions to win victories that move the United States towards greater democracy.

RESOLUTION ON CORPORATIONS

The pernicious doctrine designating corporations as artificial persons has given them a degree of power exceeding that of natural persons. We should examine and pursue, in coalition with groups such as Programs on Corporations, Law and Democracy (POCLAD) and Alliance for Democracy, ways to reduce and eventually limit this power by defining persons only as living individuals.

[PDF page 1] 2011 Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) National Convention Priorities Resolution **************************** I. DSA’s Activist Agenda: Building Movements for Economic Justice DSA will participate in social movements and protest activity that demand jobs for all and the expansion of public funding of basic human needs through the restoration of progressive income and corporate taxation, and ending the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and cuts to unnecessary military hardware spending. DSA will deepen its already significant presence, around the nation, within the Occupy Wall Street movement, as we welcome it as a major form of resistance to corporate power and the neoliberal ∗political class who accommodate it. Every DSA local and YDS chapter will decide which struggles to join depending upon their groups’ capacity, existing activist commitments, and their analysis of local political conditions and opportunities. In general, DSA locals should work in one or more of the following priority areas: a. Grassroots opposition to any long-term “budget compromise” that fails to sustain vital social programs; b. Coalitions fighting for full employment and a massive public jobs program; c. Movements fighting to prevent further disastrous cutbacks in state and local budgets, particularly to public higher education; and d. Movements fighting corporate America’s attack on the labor movement and the rights of working people, both at home and abroad, and the role the destruction of labor rights has played in causing the current global economic crisis. II. Public Educational Initiatives for Economic Justice a. The NPC has developed an ambitious “Economic Justice through Economic Education Project” that aims to “train the trainers” (grassroots activists, including DSAers) to critique neoliberal ideology and put forth a progressive, socialist-feminist alternative economic policy. b. The 50th Anniversary of The Other America Project. The convention also endorses the NPC’s efforts to create a significant educational and political project around the 50th Anniversary of The Other America and Michael Harrington’s role in initiating the War on Poverty. ∗ Neoliberalism is a worldview that favors the private sector over government and a policy agenda that supports privatization, deregulation, tax cuts, and union-busting. 1

[PDF page 2] c. DSA locals will continue to advocate and engage in educational work in regard to the structural problems of a capitalist economy and the potential for a full transition to a democratic socialist economy. III. Electoral Work in 2012 and beyond DSA locals do more social movement work and educational activities than concerted electoral work. But where they engage in electoral action, they mostly work to elect progressive Democrats (and sometimes independents) who come out of and represent grassroots struggles for social justice. We also recognize that it is crucial to work to re-elect the most progressive voices in Congress. Thus, in our PAC activity we will work to aid the re-election efforts of Senator Bernard Sanders (I-VT) and Congressman John Conyers (D-MI). IV. Building Organizational Capacity One Brick at A Time a. The DSA national office, NPC, and local activists will prioritize strengthening existing DSA locals and YDS chapters and building new ones. b. To expand our organizing capacity and achieve such growth, the DSA NPC will strengthen its Local Development and Program Committee (and recruit non-NPC members to their ranks) as well as the various DSA commissions. c. DSA and YDS will make a concerted effort to promote the movement of YDS activists into existing DSA locals or YDS graduates starting new DSA locals. d. DSA and YDS will organize DSA and YDS contingents at key national and regional gatherings of progressives. e. The NPC and national staff will organize a DSA Membership Drive to conclude at the 2013 national convention. f. DSA and YDS will act to develop their on-line capabilities, including by updating the DSA website and improving the use of social networking. g. Finally, this convention recognizes the need to integrate fundraising and budgeting into every level of DSA’s work, including DSA local and YDS chapters. *************************** Preamble: Building a Socialist Presence within Social Movements The politics of the United States has too long been characterized by a highly racialized body politic and the existence of a center and a Right, but no effective Left. As a result, amidst the greatest economic downturn since the Great Depression, the Obama administration counsels a “moderate” form of fiscal austerity as its alternative to even more inhumane Republican proposals for slashing social programs which support those who need them the most – the elderly 2

[PDF page 3] and children. Over the summer of 2011, President Obama appeared to be running for re-election as “the only adult in the room” willing to make “the painful sacrifices” to restore “long-term fiscal balance.” But his “responsible” program of extensive budget cuts and insufficient tax increases on the rich and corporations will leave tens of millions of Americans unemployed and severely weaken Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security. Perhaps realizing belatedly that his re-election chances will be heavily tied to the employment picture over the next twelve months, the administration in September 2011 advanced a modest stimulus program to be paid for by tax hikes on the rich. But the Republicans will resist even these modest efforts to revive a flagging economy -- proposals that may well be too little too late. Fortunately, the emergence of an international “Occupy Wall Street” movement signals that masses of ordinary people understand that there is no solution to this crisis without greater democratic control over the economy. President Obama’s unwillingness to take on the “Wall Street Consensus” means that he has failed to use his bully pulpit to educate Americans that the economic crisis results not from excessive social spending, but from economic deregulation, the “casino” nature of a finance- driven economy, wasteful military spending, and thirty years of regressive tax giveaways to the rich and corporate America. An electorate faced with a choice between a moderate who prioritizes “fiscal responsibility” and a conservative Republican may well opt for the more aggressive budget slasher. Nevertheless, ordinary Americans care about jobs, affordable housing, and real living standards more than they do budget deficits. What we do know is that the powers that be in Washington, D.C., will not respond adequately to mass unemployment and widespread foreclosures until there is a much greater degree of protest against this economic misery. DSA has long played a role as a “leaven” within the broader Left; our stronger locals engage in effective grassroots activism while bringing to the social movements a systemic analysis of the role of class, race, and gender oppression under capitalism. Over the last two years DSA has continued renewing and revitalizing itself to meet the challenge of making the socialist tradition relevant to 21st-century America. Membership has grown steadily for several years; new DSA locals and YDS chapters have been created; a new young National Director has begun work. The ability of many DSA locals and YDS chapters to play an immediate role in the Occupy Wall Street movement demonstrates a significant growth in our organizational capacity – a capacity that we must continue to build. While DSA recognizes that many progressive Democrats in federal and state office represent the trade union, Black, Latino, feminist and other progressive constituencies, we have no illusion as to the corporate piper who calls the tune of political elites. DSA understands that neither moral imperatives nor a correct analysis of our economic woes will cause politicians to enact the policies we need. Thus, over the next two years, DSA at both the national and local level will prioritize an educational and activist program that will build the protest politics that alone can move American politics to the left. To do this, the 2011 convention also recommends that DSA continue to take concrete steps to revitalize and strengthen our activist capacity, both in DSA and in YDS. I. DSA’s Activist Agenda: Building Movements for Economic Justice 3

[PDF page 4] Thus, the 2011 DSA national convention resolves that DSA’s number one political priority over the next two years be to deepen popular struggles against the neoliberal politics of “fiscal austerity.” This two-party consensus manifested itself in the reactionary “budget compromise” of the summer of 2011 and in the likely proposals of the Congressional Super Committee (which will prioritize slashing vital social programs over cutting the military budget and restoring progressive income and corporate taxation to the pre-Reagan era). To counter this neo-liberal consensus DSA will prioritize: Participating in social movements and protest activity that demand jobs for all and the expansion of public funding of basic human needs through the restoration of progressive income and corporate taxation, and ending the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and cuts to unnecessary military hardware. DSA locals and YDS chapters, aided by educational materials and strategic guidance from the NPC and National Office, will endeavor to be “present in every struggle” that pushes for national and state policies that prioritize jobs and human needs. We place a particular priority on working within the Occupy Wall Street movement and broadening its social base by working to build coalitions between it and the labor movement, feminist organizations, progressive electoral organizations, and community groups active in the inner city and other communities of color. DSA, nationally and locally, will work to bring “socialist value-added” to the campaigns outlined below by emphasizing that the current crisis results from a thirty-year class war by corporate elites against the rights of working people around the globe. On a global scale, the inability of working people to buy the very goods their enhanced productivity produces led to the indebtedness and fiscal and trade imbalances that caused the Great Recession. The disastrous results of this global class war, initiated by elites obsessed with driving up short-term corporate profit margins, can only be reversed if working people rebuild their own institutions and political capacity, both at home and abroad. Working people can only truly govern their destiny when they achieve democratic control of the wealth their labor (paid and unpaid) creates – by building a democratic socialist society. Every DSA local and YDS chapter will decide which struggles to join depending upon their groups’ capacity, existing activist commitments, and their analysis of local political conditions and opportunities. In general, DSA locals should work in one or more of the following priority areas: a. Grassroots opposition to any long-term “budget compromise” that fails to sustain vital social programs, such as Social Security and truly universal public health care. DSA locals and YDS chapters will build a socialist presence within the most vibrant local coalitions fighting for sane national and local priorities, be that working with Jobs With Justice, U.S. Uncut, the National Nurses/Progressive Democrats of America campaign to “Tax Wall Street and Fund Main Street” or Move-On’s “Rebuild the American Dream” campaign 4

complete_text: [PDF page 1] DSA Endorses Occupy Wall Street Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) endorses the Occupy Wall Street movement and its demand for justice. We join the demonstrators in taking a stand against corporate power and neoliberal politicians. These protests have been condemned in the press as class warfare, but in the words of a protestor on Wall Street, “they only call it class warfare when we fight back.” It was class war under the Carter administration when the government deregulated the airline, trucking, rail, communications and finance industries in favor of capitalists over workers and consumers. It was class war when Ronald Reagan fired over 11,000 striking air traffic controllers and signaled the beginning of an era of relentless union busting by employers. It was class war under the Reagan administration when the government dramatically cut taxes on the rich and raised them on the poor, while slashing Social Security survivor and disability benefits. It was class war under the Clinton administration when the government repealed the Glass-Steagall Act, legalized over-the-counter derivatives trading, crippled cash assistance to single parents with infant children, raised taxes on Social Security benefits and engineered the pro-business North American Free Trade Agreement. It was class war under the George W. Bush administration when the government further cut taxes on the rich, engineered unnecessary foreign war while ignoring domestic need, and bailed out the very banks that caused the financial crisis with trillions of dollars of taxpayers' money. It was class war under the Obama administration when the government extended the Bush tax cuts, bailed out the banks without any strings attached, failed to end foreclosures, and drastically slashed funding for essential federal programs. It was class warfare when the Supreme Court decided to lift all restrictions on corporate involvement in political campaigns. We must draw on the great traditions of resistance in our history - the Patriots, the Abolitionists, the Suffragists, Industrial Unionism, the Civil Rights Movement, and the feminist and LGBTQ movements - and engage our creative imagination in forming a movement for the 2010s. We must bear witness, but we must moreover build power that can challenge the commanding heights of capitalism and can succeed in changing laws in the people's favor. We must make demands on the state, and we must win. In the spirit of solidarity, we encourage the movement to demand: • A public jobs program • The nationalization of failed banks • Medicare for all • The forgiveness of student debt • An end to foreclosures • Substantial investment in clean energy • A fair & progressive, income & corporate tax structure • A tax on all speculative financial transactions We can fund these vital public policies if we reverse the Bush and Reagan tax cuts for the top two per cent, restore effective corporate taxation, and end wasteful military spending. And we can only reverse the decline in working people's standard of living if we restore the democratic right of working people to unionize. This is the crossroads of our age. Before us lie two divergent paths. One leads to further domination of capital and the descent of our society into a world of “have-nots” dominated by a handful of “have-lots,” a world where the government values bombs over books, where the poor pay more taxes than the rich, where environmental destruction continues to accelerate, and where racist, patriarchal and homophobic structures grow stronger. The other path leads towards greater freedom and democracy, guided by the vision of a democratic society. We must refuse to continue down the established road of increasing injustice and instead choose the difficult trek towards liberation. As Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. said, we are facing a choice between ”chaos or community,” and we must choose community. The Democratic Socialists of America enthusiastically support the Occupy Wall Street movement. Together, all the democratic forces of the 99% can remake our society, and remodel it in keeping with our age-old values of liberty, equality and solidarity. Let us show them that "we the people" are still a force to be reckoned with!

complete_text: [PDF page 1] Resolution on DSA’s Position on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer (LGBTQ) Rights 1. DSA calls for the legalization of same-sex marriages in all the States and Territories of the United States of America; the enactment of anti-discrimination laws in housing, jobs, education, and health care; and the repeal of state sodomy laws and anti-lesbian and gay restrictions. 2. DSA is committed to confronting anti-gay prejudice in its ranks and supports all efforts toward fostering understanding and cooperation among persons and groups of differing sexual orientations and identities. 3. DSA supports making public schools safe and bias-free for LGBTQ students, defending their free speech in school, and allowing students to start gay-straight alliance clubs. 4. DSA advocates for local and federal non-discrimination laws and insists that religious beliefs cannot be used to justify bias. 5. DSA supports the rights of LGBTQ parents and endorses challenging discriminatory laws that restrict the rights of LGBTQ people to parent. 6. DSA advocates for changes in the immigration system to recognize same-sex relationships including marriages, domestic partnerships, and long-standing relationships on the same basis as heterosexual relationships in approving visas, residency and citizenship. 7. The DSA, gathered in Convention 2011, welcomes the creation of a Commission to advocate for LGBTQ rights, coordinate efforts with like-minded groups, publish papers and pamphlets, support legislation to abolish discrimination against the LGBTQ community, among other activities.

Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) recognizes the importance of the institution of collective bargaining to the betterment of the conditions of workers and their unions, regardless of sector of employment. 2. DSA is committed to preserving and extending democracy throughout our society, including throughout the workplace, regardless of sector. 3. DSA recognizes that the ability to collectively bargain for better workplace conditions, salaries, and benefits improves the condition of working people not just at those workplaces, but throughout society as they are empowered to come together to better the conditions of all working men and women. 4. As amended per Virginia Code, Titles 40.1-52 thru 40.1-76 and 40.1-57.2: "No state, county, municipal, or like governmental officer, agent or governing body is vested with or possesses any authority to recognize any labor union or other employee association as a bargaining agent of any public officers or employees, or to collectively bargain or enter into any collective bargaining contract with any such union or association or its agents with respect to any matter relating to them or their employment or service." (Background: this law was passed by the Democratic-majority Virginia General Assembly and signed by Democratic Governor L. Douglas Wilder during the 1993 Legislative Session.) 5. DSA feels that, while holding its 2011 National Convention in the Commonwealth of Virginia, it is important to recognize that Virginia's public employees currently do not enjoy the rights to Collective Bargaining now extended to public employees in all but 4 states in the United States. 6. DSA opposes all existing and proposed bans on collective bargaining rights for public employees and will work to prevent or overturn them wherever possible.

The newly-elected National Political Committee with National Director Maria Svart and Deputy Director David Duhalde. (Peg Strobel, NPC member, not in photo) Photo Credit: Reid Jenkins

By Barbara Joye

DSA and YDS delegates from across the country set the organization’s course for the coming years, shared skills and insights in numerous workshops and joined in song during a three-day convention Nov. 13-15 at a retreat center in rural Pennsylvania. The attendees agreed that the “Bernie moment,” which has enabled DSA’s accelerated growth in recent months – reflected in increased attendance compared to previous conventions, justifies optimism about the future of democratic socialism in the U.S. and of DSA in particular.

[Maria Svart delivering her National Director’s report (left) and Group Photo (right)]

“It was the best DSA convention I’ve been to!” said veteran National Political Committee member David Green from Detroit DSA. He was re-elected together with seven other incumbents, who were joined by six new members. Six members are now under the age of 32, continuing the transfer of leadership to a new generation, which has been underway in recent years and was also reflected in a significant contingent of YDS members and recent YDS “graduates” attending the convention.

Most previous conventions were held in major metropolitan areas and included an evening of public speeches and entertainment, but this one focused more on internal matters. Notably, the delegates voted to approve a new, detailed strategy document, culminating a two-year period of dialogue and debate, which included numerous conference calls and a “virtual” discussion that brought together some 100 members last May. The document will be edited for style, posted on the website and distributed to members, followed by a much shorter version for use in outreach. (The previous document outlining our strategy was updated in the late 1990s.)

[Intersectionality plenary with Michele Rossi, Natalie Midiri, and Jack Suria Linares (left) and Young Democratic Socialists meeting (right)]

The convention also passed the customary “priorities resolution,” which guides the national staff in its use of the organization’s limited financial and personnel resources. The priorities included 1) building DSA and increasing public awareness of democratic socialism through grassroots work for Bernie Sanders (but independent of his official campaign); 2) implementing the approaches to organizing laid out in the strategy document; 3) increasing DSA involvement in local anti-racist coalitions; 4) electoral work to defeat the Right while building the Left and a stronger DSA; and 5) rethinking our organizing practices and structures to facilitate our longer-range strategy. The priorities resolution will be posted on the DSA website, along with resolutions supporting local work to promote public banks, use of social media to build DSA and support Internet democracy, and a DSA Environmental Justice Network. [Update: See below for the priorities resolution.]

Two new working groups were established in addition to the one addressing the environment: one charged with reviewing DSA’s approach to international issues (including membership in the Socialist International), and a social media committee. Those interested in joining these groups should contact the national office.

The 2016-17 National Political Committee elected members are: Jared Abbott, Hope Adair, Theresa Alt, David Green, José Gutierrez, Elizabeth Henderson, Frank Llewellyn, Sean Monahan, Simone Morgen, Brandon Payton-Carrillo, Joe Schwartz, Peg Strobel and Russell Weiss-Irwin. The convention also voted to add two new honorary vice chairs: Deborah Meier and Bhaskar Sunkara.

Barbara Joye is a member of Metro Atlanta DSA.

National Political Committee (NPC) Priorities Resolution Passed at the 2015 DSA National Convention

Whereas national conventions set the main political and organizational priorities that govern national DSA work over the ensuing two years, particularly the time and resources of national staff and the elected national political leadership devoted to these tasks;

And whereas the campaign of democratic socialist Bernie Sanders for the Democratic Party presidential nomination provides a unique opportunity to enhance public knowledge of democratic socialism and to recruit for and strengthen DSA;

And whereas the completion of the new DSA strategy document provides the opportunity to educate our members and interested parties as to the role of a socialist organization in the United States – and to recruit to and build that organization,

Be It Resolved That:

National DSA resources and leadership and staff time will be primarily devoted to the following five areas:

1. Building DSA through the Sanders campaign

To accomplish that task, the NPC and national staff, working with the national DSA Sanders Committee, will help locals and future locals to

a. table and canvass with DSA materials related to the Sanders effort

b. engage in effective recruitment to DSA of people who sign up through DSA tabling and canvassing efforts

c. organize well-publicized DSA forums (or co-sponsored forums) on such topics as “Sanders and Building a Socialist Movement” and “Building a More Racially and Class-Diverse Sanders Campaign”

d. develop broad, multi-racial coalitions that can continue the work of the Sanders movement after the campaign is over. Such coalitions are essential to building a stronger U.S. left and a stronger socialist current within that left

In fulfilling these goals, DSA locals and activists will emphasize in their Sanders work the need to emerge from the campaign with a stronger socialist organization (DSA) and an increased socialist presence within U.S. politics. The Sanders campaign has raised public consciousness as to how unrestrained corporate power subverts democracy. DSA’s task is to increase public awareness of the democratic socialist alternative to capitalism

The national organization will provide training in the skills necessary for this work including training for one-on-one recruitment

The national organization will set local and YDS goals to ensure that work is not only done but also evaluated

The national organization will consider (weighing our limited resources) organizing activities inside and outside of the Democratic National Convention aimed at recruiting Sanders delegates to DSA and at recruiting activists in the streets who will be demanding that the Democrats advance a pro-labor economic and racial justice program

DSA will also work in the Sanders movement to broaden the racial, class, and gender base of the Sanders movement and to build local progressive coalitions and relationships with organizations and protest movements that last beyond the campaign

2. Building the Organization by Implementing Our Strategy

Over the next two years the national leadership and staff will aid our locals in expanding their activist core – and the skills of that core — so that the organization can begin to implement the strategy document at the local and state level

The National Office (NO) and NPC will work with each local and YDS chapter to develop a concrete plan to build a more visible and effective socialist organization in their localities. Locals should come up with a feasible set of tasks to increase their capacity do “mass work” or “coalition politics” while bringing a unique socialist perspective to the work. DSA locals will work to advance this socialist perspective through public and internal education and by injecting more demands for anti-corporate measures and non-reformist reforms into our coalition work.

When possible, the national organization will aid stronger locals in developing their own projects that are complementary to existing progressive projects so that we can maximize our own visibility as socialists (e.g., campaigns for public banks or for financial transaction taxes to finance expanded public goods or for living wage legislation)

This work will include developing study guide materials for reading and study groups to discuss the strategy document and the issues in socialist vision, analysis, and strategy raised therein

3. Increasing DSA Involvement in Local Anti-Racist Coalition Work

To build a stronger, more diverse Left—and ultimately a more diverse socialist organization—democratic socialists must increase their involvement in coalitions fighting for racial justice

The NPC and national staff will develop materials and training to aid our locals in engaging in more anti-racist coalition work. The national organization will also help locals to develop knowledge of their local political communities, as well as to enhance their organizing and political skills. Depending on local circumstances, anti-racist work may involve joining struggles against mass incarceration and police brutality; the fight to defend and expand voting rights; struggles for more equitable public education (e.g., campaigns to end “the school to prison pipeline”); and/or the fight for immigrant rights

4. Electoral Work in 2016: Defeating the Right, while Building the Left and a Stronger DSA

While building the socialist wing of a stronger Left, we also recognize the importance of defeating the increasingly successful right-wing campaign to control state and national governments at the executive, legislative, and judicial levels. Such control threatens basic labor, voting, immigrant, and reproductive rights

Thus, our electoral strategy will have two primary components: building a stronger socialist electoral presence in U.S politics, and defeating the right and center’s unconscionable attacks on the welfare state, labor rights, immigrant rights, and reproductive justice.

In the summer and fall of 2016 DSA locals will engage strategically in electoral work, depending on local circumstances. Where Democrats face serious challenges from the extreme right, locals may work to ensure electoral victory over Republicans. Where Democrats do not face such a threat our focus may be either on supporting left-wing Democratic candidates in primary challenges against centrist Democrats or in supporting independent socialist and other third-party candidates (often in non-partisan local races) if they serve to strengthen independent socialist electoral capacity

In either case, we will use these campaigns as opportunities to push substantive issues (such as raising the minimum wage, expanding basic democratic rights and participation, reversing climate change and increasing community oversight of police) as well as to build ties between diverse progressive constituencies that can be deepened after the election is over.

5. Rethinking our Organizing Practices and Structures

We will also evaluate how our organizing practices and organizational structures can be best adapted to facilitate our longer-range strategy.

Minutes of the 2025 DSA Nat’l Convention Approved for release by vote of the National Political Committee on October 1, 2025. The biennial National Convention of the Democratic Socialists of America was held from Friday, August 8, 2025 to Sunday, August 10, 2025 at McCormick Place in Chicago, IL, with Convention Planning Committee Co-chairs Laura W (Portland, OR) and Chris W (Seattle) presiding. The Convention was called to order at 9:00 am by Co-chair Laura W. The appointed Chair presiding over the first session was Alex M of Seattle. Friday, August 8, 2025 The DSA National Political Committee Co-chairs delivered opening remarks, with Ashik S (at-large) giving the first speech and Megan R (at-large) giving the second. The speeches from the Co-chairs reflected on the previous two years and their hopes for DSA in the next two years. The NPC Treasurer, John L (New Orleans) delivered a summary of the Budget and Finance Committee reports, which can be found under the Reports heading below. Credentials Subcommittee Co-chair Matt M of Pittsburgh delivered the Credentials Report, offering recommendations on challenges against delegations from Birmingham, AL; Los Angeles, CA; Delaware and the Queens, NY branch of NYC-DSA. The assembly accepted the recommendations on the challenges and the roster of delegates presented by the Credentials Committee by unanimous consent. CPC Co-chair Chris W moved adoption of the Convention Rules, noting the reduction of the threshold to remove items from the Consent Agenda from a majority vote to just 40 percent of delegates present and voting. Resolutions Subcommittee member Richard S from Baltimore moved an amendment to require masking while in the Convention Hall to prevent the spread of airborne disease. The amendment was rejected by a vote of 459 in the affirmative and 493 in the negative. The Convention Rules, unamended, were adopted by unanimous consent. Programming Subcommittee Co-chair Hayley BB (Portland) moved adoption of the Convention Agenda. The Chair ruled, upon advice of the Parliamentarian, that R06, One Member, One Vote for Federal Endorsements was contradicted by Article XIII of the DSA Bylaws and should be removed from General Orders as not being in good order. Ben D of Metro DC appealed from the decision of the Chair and gave a brief speech defending the resolution as consistent with customary practice in DSA, followed by the Chair’s rebuttal which focused on the language in the bylaws and his interpretation of the parliamentary authority. The ruling of the Chair was sustained by the Delegates, 669-501. Next, NPC Co-chair Ashik S moved an amendment to General Orders to promote CR03, CR07, CR09, and R24 much higher in the list while demoting R44 much lower in the list. Once stack was exhausted, the amendment was lost by a vote of 507 to 651. The Convention Agenda, including its unamended list of General Orders, was then adopted by unanimous consent. The Chair then moved adoption of the Consent Agenda as recommended by the CPC as the first Special Order of the day. With no objections or speeches against, the Consent Agenda was adopted by unanimous consent. The first General Order was CB03, Setting Fee Structures for the Organization’s Print Publications, moved by Faye W of San Francisco. The amendment would modernize the provisions of the bylaws governing DSA’s official publications, which were written based on the assumption of physical and not digital printing and distribution. With no objections or speeches against, the bylaws amendment was adopted by unanimous consent. Next, the assembly considered CB04, Fair Representation via STV Delegate Elections, moved by Ringo X of Worcester. The amendment would universalize Scottish Single Transferable Vote as the method that every chapter must use to elect delegates to the National Convention. After debate, the bylaws amendment was adopted by a vote of 711 in the affirmative and 412 in the negative. Around noon, the assembly heard the Convention’s keynote speech delivered by US Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan’s 12th Congressional District and member of Metro Detroit DSA. The speech denounced the genocide in Gaza and the collaboration of her colleagues in that crime, in the provision of weapons, logistical support, and diplomatic cover. The Representative emphasized the need for a clear political alternative that will not compromise on the fundamental humanity of the Palestinian people. The well-received speech was followed by a brief performance by the NYC-DSA choir. The Convention then recessed for lunch around 12:30 pm. After lunch and convention programming the delegates reconvened at 2:00 pm, with Brian W of Metro DC relieving Alex M of appointed Chair duties. Deliberation resumed with CB01, Democracy Commission Comprehensive Structural Reform Proposal, moved by Democracy Commission Steering Committee member Aaron B (at-large). The Democracy Commission was created by the 2023 Convention to bring proposals to the 2025 Convention, and its members were elected from the general membership by the delegates to the 2023 Convention. Their proposal consisted of 10 individual pieces offered as an omnibus, one of which had already been adopted on the Consent Agenda. Each one of the planks addressed different areas in DSA’s internal administration and democracy, from how membership is counted, to the size of the board of directors, and the definition of committees, commissions, and working groups, just to name a few elements of the omnibus. Delegate Zeke D of Seattle rose to demand division of the question on CB01, to consider CB01-6, Changes to the NPC, and CB01-9, Rechartering the Democracy Commission, pursuant to RONR 12th ed. 27:10. The Chair considered the division of the question on demand not well taken, claiming that the amendment period preceding the Convention was the appropriate time to suggest or reject changes to the constitutional and bylaws amendments in CB01 and the ruling was appealed. The ruling of the Chair that the question would not be divided on demand was sustained by a vote of 909 in the affirmative to 260 in the negative. The question before the assembly returned to CB01 undivided. After debate, and a call for the previous question that failed with 718 in the affirmative and 457 in the negative, the omnibus proposal was adopted by vote of 989 in the affirmative and 217 in the negative. CB02, One Member, One Vote for National Leadership, as amended by CB02-A01: Power to the Members: Deliberative Democracy for One Member One Vote on the Consent Agenda, was then moved by Carl R of Metro DC. The constitutional amendment would require the election of the NPC and select national leadership by secret ballot of all members in good standing. During debate, Delegate Richard S of Baltimore moved to vacate the Chair. After the Chair clarified that he would be relieved of duty after the vote on the main motion, the motion to vacate was withdrawn before it was seconded. Debate on CB02 continued, and a vote to extend debate failed with 672 in the affirmative and 455 in the negative. The main motion was lost by vote of 487 in the affirmative and 736 in the negative. Brian W was relieved of appointed Chair duties by Ian G of Milwaukee after the vote on CB02 was tabulated and announced. The next General Order was R27: Staff Relationship to Members in a Democratic Organization, moved by Programming Subcommittee Co-chair and former DSA staffer Hayley BB. The resolution would clarify the expectations around staff’s political activity inside DSA, and would establish that all records of the organization will be accessible to members of the NPC and their designees. After debate, the resolution was adopted by a vote of 683 to 494. Next was R44: Resolution on Staff, Contractors, and Budgeting, moved by David J of New York City. The resolution would place a cap on personnel expenses preventing the NPC from allocating more than 40 percent of the operating budget on compensation for staff or contractors. The question immediately moved to R44-A01, For a Member-Guided Budgeting Process, which was moved by Budget and Finance Committee Co-chair Shane K of Baltimore. The amendment focused on transparency and accountability in the budgeting process itself. After debate, the amendment to R44 was adopted by a vote of 627 to 492. A scheduled recess then interrupted consideration of R44 as amended. Before the Convention recessed at 6:00 pm, delegates heard announcements explaining the NPC Co-chair elections process and the speaker lottery for the Political Exchange on Saturday. The Co-chair election ran from 6:00 pm to 10:00 pm, and so did the entry period for the speaker lottery. The assembly reconvened at 6:30 pm with Griffin M of Metro DC relieving Ian G of appointed Chair duties. The question returned to R44 as amended by R44-A01. After debate, the main motion as amended failed narrowly, 583 to 594, the closest recorded margin of the Convention. The next order of business was R35, For Working-Class Member Leadership, moved by NPC member Alex P of New York City. The resolution instructs the NPC to provide stipends to members of the NPC Steering Committee and the Co-chairs of the Communications Committee and National Labor Commission. No specific amount was specified. The debate moved to amendment R35-A01, Stipend the NPC, which would restrict stipends to NPC members or YDSA National Coordinating Committee members at a maximum of $1000 per month. After debate, the amendment was rejected by a vote of 538-642. The question on the floor returned to R35, unamended, and after debate was exhausted the resolution was adopted by vote of 651-501. The next item in General Orders was CR05, National Electoral Commission Consensus Resolution, moved by Hayley BB of Portland. The consensus resolution was previously amended by CR05-A04: Carnation Program Amendment to the NEC Resolution and CR05-A05: Invest in Cadre Candidates and Political Independence, both of which carried on the Consent Agenda. The resolution itself had four sections regarding candidate recruitment, endorsement criteria, the creation of a Socialists in Office Committee, and a recommendation to end “paper endorsements” across all chapters. Debate then proceeded to CR05-A02, One DSA: Toward a Unified Endorsement Process, which was moved by Ethan E of NYC. The amendment would remove the distinction between a local chapter endorsement of a candidate and a national organization endorsement. After debate, the amendment failed by a vote of 373-794. This was the last item considered by the delegates before the Convention adjourned for the day at 8:00 pm, 11 hours after the first gavel. Saturday, August 9, 2025 The convention’s second day was called to order by CPC Co-chair Chris W at 9:00 am, with the announcement of the NPC Co-chair election results. The announcement was delivered by Aaron B of the Rules and Elections Subcommittee. Incumbents Megan R and Ashik S were re-elected to another two year term. After the announcement Jacey L of Connecticut assumed the duties of appointed Chair. Deliberation returned to CR05, the National Electoral Commission Consensus Resolution (at this point only amended by amendments on the Consent Agenda) which was left pending the previous day. The next amendment, CR05-A03: Towards Deliberative Federal Endorsements, was moved by Chanpreet S (Seattle) of the National Electoral Commission. The amendment added language that detailed the endorsement process itself as a form of consultation between the NEC and NPC where the former advises the latter as a body. After debate, the amendment was adopted 655-525. The debate then returned to the main motion, CR05: National Electoral Commission Consensus Resolution, as amended by CR05-A03 and CR05-A04 and CR05-A05 on the consent agenda. After debate, the consensus resolution as amended carried by a vote of 1049-132. The next item in general order was R33: Unite Labor & the Left to Run a Socialist For President and Build the Party. Nate K of Atlanta rose to a point of order, pointing out that the next item in General Orders (R33) contained a similar provision to R06, which was ruled out of order for contradicting Article XIII of the Bylaws, and should also be removed from consideration. The Chair considered the point of order well taken, ruling that R33 was out of order for the same reason that R06 was out of order. The decision of the Chair was appealed on the grounds that a substitute amendment to R33 which lacked a polling provision existed, and that unlike R06, the content of R33 alone went above and beyond a poll of the members. At this point Veronica D of River Valley, MA. assumed the Chair to dispose of the appeal. The Chair’s ruling was overturned by a majority in a show of voting cards. A call for division of the house was not heard for lack of a proper second. Jacey L resumed the chair at this point. Subsequently, a Delegate from Metro DC moved to vacate the Chair, which was properly seconded. After consulting with the parliamentarian, CPC co-chair Chris W presided over the vote, which was conducted by show of voting cards. The motion to vacate the appointed Chair failed. Before yielding the position of Chair, Chris W reminded the Delegates to treat the Chair, Jacey L, with the same respect that they treated chairs Alex M, Brian W, Ian G, and Griffin M. Jacey L then resumed the duties of appointed Chair. Debate resumed on R33, and delegate Alex P of NYC-DSA was recognized to motivate the resolution, which calls for a broad left-labor coalition in a type of popular front to run a socialist for President of the US and creates an exploratory committee to that end with instructions to produce a resolution for consideration at the 2027 convention. By way of contrast, R33-A02: Building a United Front Toward 2028 (formerly R37), as it says in the title, calls for a united front of leftist organizations and centers the demand for a general strike in 2028 over a presidential campaign. The amendment was motivated by Luisa M of Portland, OR. After debate, the amendment failed 631-540. The main motion, unamended, was adopted 687-471. After a 30 minute break, deliberation resumed at 11:00 am, with Veronica D relieving Jacey L of appointed chair duties. Immediately upon reconvening the Chair ruled on a motion to suspend the rules to add a debate block from 2:00 pm to 3:00 pm as out of order. The Chair’s ruling was sustained by a vote of 853-266. For the next four items in General Orders, Veronica D requested that CPC Co-chair Chris W preside, which was accepted. The next question was R20: Workers Will Lead the Way: Join with Unions to Run Labor Candidates, moved by Jeremy C of NYC-DSA. This resolution would commit DSA to running a slate of at least 10 labor candidates for public office in the 2026 election cycle, from a diversity of industrial sectors. Debate moved immediately to R20-A01: Democratic Socialists and the Labor Movement Need Each Other which clarified that this campaign would be housed in the National Electoral Commission specifically and emphasized the democratic socialist identification of those candidates. The motion was introduced by Annie W of River Valley, MA. After debate it was adopted 834-315. R20 was adopted as amended by vote of 987-89. Continuing the theme of organized labor, the next item was CR10: DSA National Labor Commission Consensus Resolution: Building A Worker-Led Labor Movement, which was considered as amended by CR10-A02, CR10-A03, and CR10-A04 on the Consent Agenda. The consensus resolution was the product of deliberation in the National Labor Commission and contained seven sections detailing the organization’s labor strategy for the next two years. Debate then moved to an amendment that was not passed on consent, CR10-A01: A Partyist Labor Strategy. It was introduced by Sarah M of Portland, OR. The amendment would go beyond the base resolution by making labor organizing a means to an end of forming a new political party. After debate, the amendment failed 544-591. The main motion as amended by its consent agenda amendments only was adopted with a vote of 1024 in the affirmative and 110 in the negative. Veronica D resumed the Chair and announced the next question, CR02: Building an Internationalist Party, moved by Jorge R of NYC-DSA. The resolution designated the Progressive International as the “political international” of DSA, and called for a national speaking tour in collaboration with PI. Further, the resolution would enable the International Committee to deepen ties with organizations based outside the US who were invited to the Convention. Debate then moved to its amendment, CR02-A02: Democratic Socialist Internationalism, introduced by Ben D of Metro DC, which would proscribe a more critical attitude towards existing leftist formations in other nations based on democratic socialist values. The amendment failed 504-655. CR02, unamended, was adopted by vote of 1013-123 after debate. R22: For a Fighting Anti-Zionist DSA was the next item in the queue, introduced by Francesa M of Connecticut. It would reaffirm a resolution referred to the 2023-2025 NPC by the 2023 Convention to “Make DSA an Anti-Zionist Organization in Principle and Praxis,” establish standards of membership that would make material support of Israel an expellable offense, and make support of BDS a basic expectation. It would also reaffirm DSA’s work in coalitions, on campuses, and in the labor movement in regards to Palestinian liberation. Finally, it would also affirm DSA’s commitment to “al-Thawabit,” the principles first promulgated by the Palestinian National Council in 1977, which claim the Palestinian right to resistance, self-determination, return from all locales to mandatory Palestine, and the recognition of Jerusalem as the capital of a Palestinian state. The debate moved directly to R22-A01: Align with the BDS Movement, moved by Layla E of Metro Detroit. The amendment would strike the language about standards for membership in DSA and the penalties for not meeting those standards, and more closely align the base resolution with the demands of the BDS Movement, as stated in the title. After debate, the amendment was lost by a vote of 572 in the affirmative and 688 in the negative. The Convention then recessed for scheduled lunch around 1:30 pm with R22, unamended, still pending. Debate was scheduled to resume the next day at 10:30 am. The afternoon saw the inaugural Cross-Organizational Political Exchange, held from 3:00 pm to 6:00 pm. Guests who spoke included the Palestinian Youth Movement, the Los Angeles Tenant Union, and Building a Fighting NALC (National Association of Letter Carriers). International guests included the Partido Socialismo e Liberdade (PSOL) from Brazil, Morena from Mexico and other socialists from Japan, Belgium, the UK and elsewhere. The Exchange was facilitated by Convention Planning Co-chair Laura W (Portland, OR) and Ramy K (Twin Cities). Speakers were given the following prompts for discussion: 1. Based on your experience in your own organization and political context, what possibilities do you see in the potential to organize against the agenda of Trump and the far-right, and also to build toward mass action on May Day, 2028? What would be needed, and what are the specific challenges? 2. DSA members have been debating the possibility of new electoral formations – such as a working-class coalition or political party – that challenge both the ruling far right (the Republican Party) and the liberal establishment (the Democratic Party). Based on what you experience in your own organization and political context, what value or risk do you see in this possibility? After the exchange, the Convention was adjourned for the day at 6:00 pm. Ballots were issued via email for the NPC At-large election around 6:00 pm. The election closed at 10:00 pm. Sunday, August 10, 2025 With convention programming running from 9:00 am to 10:20 am, the Delegates did not resume deliberations until 10:30 am. Rory G of Chicago presided over the final session as appointed Chair. The session opened with the question left pending at the close of business yesterday, R22: For a Fighting Anti-Zionist DSA, unamended. Interrupting consideration was a motion to suspend the rules to consider extending debate until 2:30 pm, cutting into scheduled meal time. The motion to suspend the rules was lost by a vote of 479 in the affirmative and 590 in the negative. After the vote to suspend the rules failed, debate returned to the main motion. Abdullah F of Los Angeles made a motion to divide the question on R22 to strike lines 28 to 51, which address the standards of membership and provisions for expulsion for failure to meet those standards. The Chair ruled that the motion to divide was dilatory, as it was substantially similar to the amendment which failed the day before, R22-A01, which struck the exact same text. The ruling of the Chair was sustained on appeal by vote of 636 in the affirmative and 499 in the negative. After the appeal was disposed of, debate on R22 itself opened for the first time since it was introduced the day before. After the stack was exhausted, the main motion was adopted 675-524. The next item was R01: DSA for One Palestinian State, moved by Alex M of Seattle. The resolution would stake DSA to a position of one secular and democratic state in mandatory Palestine. As indicated by its number, this resolution was the first to meet the signature requirement for consideration at Convention. There were two amendments that qualified for consideration, the first being R01-A01: DSA for Palestinian Self-Determination, moved by Nayef A of San Francisco. This amendment would remove language about the character of a future unified Palestinian state and replace it with language about the right to self-determination in government. It would additionally reframe the conflict in Palestine as primarily settler-colonial and not religious in nature. After debate, the amendment failed 565-620. Delegates next considered R01-A02: DSA Endorses the One Democratic State Campaign, moved by Elisha A (Tacoma-Pierce County). Essentially a substitute, this amendment would replace much of the language of the base resolution with an endorsement of the One Democratic State Campaign, as stated in the title. This Palestinian-led campaign produced a 10-point manifesto that reiterates the right of return, calls for a single democratic and constitutional state between the river and sea, and a guarantee of collective and individual rights for all. After debate, the amendment failed 526-652. Debate returned to the main motion after the failure of both amendments. The main motion, unamended, failed 330-752. It bears mentioning that the endorsement of the al-Thawabit principles with the adoption of R22 reflects DSA’s position on the Palestinian national question. Next, Griffin M moved R42: Labor for an Arms Embargo, which would prioritize the DSA National Labor Commission campaign of the same name as the primary demand of the organization as a whole in relation to the struggle for Palestinian liberation, and includes a call to run congressional candidates to back that demand. Debate subsequently moved to its amendment, R42-A01: For a Strike Ready Labor for an Arms Embargo, which would emphasize the tactic of striking to win the demand of an arms embargo by directly disrupting the United States arms supply chain, and remove the call to run candidates for US Congress. It failed 421-770. Debate returned to the main motion, unamended, and after stack was exhausted, the resolution was adopted by show of voting cards. A call for division of the house was ruled dilatory, as the Chair claimed that there was no reasonable doubt as to which side prevailed on the question. The decision of the Chair was sustained by a show of voting cards. The next question before the assembly was R34: Workers Deserve More, Forever: For a Coherent and Continuous Program Befitting DSA’s Political Growth, which would enshrine the Workers Deserve Program as the official political platform of DSA (replacing the one first adopted in 2021) and establish a new committee to consider revisions to be brought to the next Convention. It was introduced by At-large Delegate Michaela B. R34-A01: A Fighting Socialist Program for DSA was next offered as a substitute to the main motion. This proposal was a merger and rewrite of proposals previously numbered R12 and R23, and reflected a collaboration between the original authors. Like the base resolution, this program would replace the 2021 platform, but also would replace Workers Deserve More as the official political program. The amendment was moved by Rashad X of San Francisco. After debate, the substitute failed 532-651. Debate then returned to the main motion unamended, and it was adopted 900-291. The final item that the Convention had time to consider was R07: Principles for Party-Building, introduced by Connell H of River Valley, MA. In line with the theme of the convention, this resolution commits DSA to the goal of becoming an independent mass socialist party, along 10 principles. After debate, the resolution was adopted by vote of 641 in the affirmative and 551 in the negative. Afterwards, the convention recessed for lunch around 1:30 pm. Constitution & Bylaws Amendments (CB) To be considered for debate at the Convention, proposed changes to the Constitution or Bylaws must have a minimum of 250 signatures of support from DSA members who are in good standing. Proposals meeting the signature requirement also become eligible for amendment prior to convention. Constitutional changes require a two-thirds (⅔) vote of the Convention to pass; Bylaws changes require a three-fifths (⅗) vote of the Convention to pass. Any member or group of DSA members in good standing may propose secondary amendments to the constitution or bylaws changes. To be considered for discussion these secondary amendments must have a minimum of 250 signatures of support from DSA members in good standing. Constitutional and Bylaws Amendments submitted by the National Political Committee with two-thirds approval may be considered even if they do not receive 250 signatures. All Constitutional and Bylaws Amendments must be finalized 30 days prior to the commencement of the Convention to meet the notice requirements. In all Constitution and Bylaws amendments, proposed additions are green and underlined, proposed deletions are red and struck out, and omitted text is unaffected. CB01: Democracy Commission Comprehensive Structural Reform Proposal Submitted by Aaron B (Southeast MN), Connell H (River Valley), Ramsin C (Chicago), Allison K (New York City), Kristian H (North Texas). Qualified on Apr 23, 2025, with 519 signatures as of May 11, 2025. Status: Adopted Introduction DSA’s 2023 Convention voted to create the Democracy Commission, a body tasked with bringing proposals reforming DSA’s national structure to the 2025 Convention. The first stage of the commission involved researching the structures of other parties as well as DSA itself to determine what is needed to make our organization more democratic and effective. DSA’s inability to address structural concerns several conventions in a row signaled the need for organizational consensus, requiring a commission that was politically representative of tendencies within DSA. Convention delegates voted for the 21 members of the Commission in an election in October 2023, resulting in a commission with members of eight different caucuses as well as uncaucused DSA members. Based on our research and discussion, the Democracy Commission developed guiding principles for our work to have a shared understanding of our goals and priorities. The guiding principles can be read in full in our report to membership; the central points of the introduction are below: * The purpose of member democracy in DSA is to empower the working class to act collectively in its own self-interest towards the project of its emancipation. * Democracy means people have power individually and collectively and requires that democratically-made decisions be carried out by organizational leadership. Democracy thrives on direct, honest, and comradely debate conducted in open meetings with meaningful stakes, where analysis is developed to inform specific strategies. * Healthy organizational democracy depends on both formal structure and rules and organizational culture. Rules should encourage and incentivize healthy habits, instincts, and norms and not merely prescribe them. They should be flexible enough to work at times of membership expansion and of contraction. Proposals by the Democracy Commission should foster a sense of shared organizational identity in the organization and among members. They should encourage horizontal relationships between chapters as well as improve member connection to DSA national. * Deliberation within DSA should be meaningful and members should be encouraged to engage with the ideas and arguments. We should encourage reconsideration of positions as a norm. A healthy democratic organization can decide on, and evolve, its shared principles and a program. * Members should be transformed through their engagement with DSA, empowered to lead and change and engage in democracy in the organization and subsequently their local community. DSA’s democratic culture should train members to intervene in democratic debates in their unions, communities, and in moments of mass struggle, to democratize workers’ movements and organizations. Based on our guiding principles, the Commission has drafted a package of reforms that, together, will improve DSA's democratic and organizational function across the organization. Everything below won a super-majority vote of the Democracy Commission. Working from the Commission’s democratically-adopted guiding principles, every proposal went through revision, compromise, negotiation, and debate before approval. No commissioner got everything and no commissioner got nothing; the omnibus is contoured by our most fundamental agreements. Positive and negative input from Commissioners across tendencies shaped each plank; each plank is specially shaped to support the overall omnibus as a single unified reform. We believe these planks will fix some structural problems with DSA. But more importantly, taken together these proposals are a vision for our organization: coming together across political disagreements to create a healthier democratic culture and structure that reduces the distance between members, chapters, and national leadership; unifies us through deliberation and decision-making, not fiat; and empowers workers to take control of our political life, on the road to taking control of our world. Removing the constitutional member category ensures there’s one category of membership and gives members more accurate membership metrics. Full text Amendments to the DSA Constitution Article III. Members Section 2. An individual shall apply to be a member following the procedure prescribed by the Bylaws. Application for membership shall be made to the Chapter or National Organization. Members are in good standing provided that they pay annual dues as prescribed in the Bylaws. Section 5. There shall be yearly dues, the amount of which shall be determined by the NPC prior to the commencement of each annual dues cycle. Amendments to the DSA Bylaws Article I. Membership Section 2. Members will receive the organizational outreach publication. Members are encouraged to participate in political activities and education. New members will receive a membership card, and renewing members shall receive such a card upon request. Members will receive information on National policy from the National Office. A member is in good standing only if their payment of dues is current. Only members in good standing are eligible to vote and to hold office in the organization. Membership in the organization may be maintained by persons who are up to one year arrears in dues. Such members may cure their arrearage and place themselves in good standing by paying their dues. Delegates to the National Convention shall be apportioned based on the dues-paying membership of the organization (including all members up to one year arrears in dues). Delegate-to-member ratios shall be set by the NPC at least six (6) months before the Convention, except in the case of Special Conventions, where such ratios shall be set by the NPC as soon as possible after the Convention is called.
