Whereas, this resolution attempts to compile all of the known grievance authority in a single place and codify the DSA practice of treating harassment and non-harassment grievances the same way under existing policy. Resolved, 1. Resolution 33 passed by the 2017 DSA National Convention and all amendments to Resolution 33 and decisions related to Resolution 33, whether passed by convention, the NPC, or otherwise, are rescinded. 2. DSA adopts the following Uniform Grievance Policy: UNIFORM GRIEVANCE POLICY Democratic Socialists of America is committed to creating a space that is welcoming and inclusive to members of all genders, races, and classes. The following policy provides guidelines to ensure that everyone is able to organize without fear of harassment, abuse, or harm. We further recognize that interpersonal conflict can arise within our organization and manifest itself within and without our political processes. The processes created by this policy are designed to address inappropriate personal conduct by members, and not political conduct which may nevertheless interfere with DSA's core political work. 1. General Provisions 1. Any investigation or proceeding by any DSA body, including but not limited to a chapter, a chapter steering committee (“SC”), or the National Political Committee (“NPC”), which may result in a member being disciplined by the organization on the basis of their personal conduct, whether permanently, temporarily, or otherwise, must follow the procedures laid out in this policy. 2. This policy does not apply to simple moderation of online resources, though a member’s conduct in online spaces may give rise to a complaint under this policy. 3. This policy does not restrict a chapter meeting’s ability to remove a member from said meeting where said member’s behavior during the meeting violates this policy or DSA’s Meeting Code of Conduct. 4. “Conflict of interest” as used in this policy means a member’s inability to participate in a grievance-related proceeding without preconceived judgment or opinions.. The mere knowledge of circumstances surrounding a grievance does not, in itself, give rise to a conflict of interest. 5. All DSA and YDSA chapters will follow this policy. Provisions of chapter bylaws or policies that directly contradict this policy are superseded by this policy. 2. Behavior and Conduct. 1. Prohibited behavior. Members shall not engage in harassment on the basis of sex, gender, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, physical appearance, disability, race, color, religion, national origin, class, age, or profession. Conduct, such as unwelcome attention, inappropriate or offensive remarks, slurs, or jokes, physical or verbal intimidation, stalking, inappropriate physical contact or proximity, and other verbal and physical conduct constitutes harassment only when one or more of the following occurs: 1. Submission to such conduct is made either explicitly or implicitly a term or condition of a member’s continued affiliation with DSA; 2. Submission or rejection of such conduct by an individual is used as the basis for organizational decisions affecting such individual; or, 3. Such conduct has the purpose or effect of creating a hostile environment interfering with an individual’s capacity to organize within DSA. 1. A “hostile environment” is created only where the conduct is sufficiently severe or pervasive as to alter the conditions of membership in DSA and create an abusive organizing environment. 2. Conduct will be presumed “sufficiently severe or pervasive” where a reasonable person would be offended by the conduct. 2. Member conduct. Members are expected to abide by the National Code of Conduct, the Meeting Code of Conduct, and any applicable bylaws provisions or code of conduct passed by their local chapter. 3. Online conduct. Expectations regarding the conduct of DSA members are enforceable for online behavior, including but not limited to conduct on social media, as well as offline behavior. 3. Harassment/Grievance Officers. 1. DSA will have harassment/grievance officers (“HGOs”) at both the local and national levels. HGOs will assist members in making complaints, investigate complaints, report the results of investigations to the appropriate body, and educate members on this policy. 4. Privileges of Membership. 1. Members of DSA are vested with the privilege of being treated with fundamental fairness during any investigation or proceeding under this policy. 2. Specifically, members are entitled: 1. To notice, in writing, of any allegations made against them. 2. To an opportunity to respond, in writing, to any allegations made against them. 3. To have complaints they make or that are made against them investigated by HGOs. 4. To the confidentiality of information they may share during an investigation or proceeding under this policy, with the understanding that any information provided during an investigation or proceeding under this policy may be shared with the Steering Committee and may be reviewed at the national level. 5. To a written final adjudication on complaints they make or that are made against them, including factual findings based on evidence, when an outcome is reached. 6. To appeal final adjudications and/or discipline to which the member is a party and which is adverse to that member to the NPC. There is no privilege of appeal from any decision of the NPC. 5. National Structures. 1. National DSA will: 1. Have and maintain a Committee of Grievance Officers (“CGO”) as described in subsection c of this section. 2. Have and maintain a National Grievance Panel (“National Grievance Panel”) as described in subsection d of this section. 2. The National Political Committee (“NPC”) will: 1. Maintain and revise as necessary the National Code of Conduct and Meeting Code of Conduct. 2. Ensure that chapters are in compliance with this policy by maintaining a list of chapter HGOs and training they attend. 3. Refrain from using any independent contractor, other than attorneys hired to represent DSA and provide DSA with legal advice, to effect the terms of this policy. 4. Have ultimate and sole authority to make decisions on complaints or appeals that may come before it. For complaints appropriately directed to the NPC, the NPC is the Steering Committee as that term is used in this policy. 5. Ensure that NGP members have access to past NPC grievance decisions while adequately protecting all potentially sensitive member data. 6. Individual members of the NPC will recuse themselves from any matter under this policy in which they have a conflict of interest, or in which a conflict of interest is likely to arise. 3. Committee of Grievance Officers. The Committee of Grievance Officers (“CGO”) will work to formalize connections between HGOs in local chapters and in YDSA for the purpose of ongoing skillshares and collaboration, and to provide HGOs support for their work. 1. Membership on the CGO is open to DSA and YDSA members in good standing who are interested in the harassment and grievance process, able to contribute to the work of the committee, and who are invited by the Steering Committee of the CGO. Members will be invited on an “as-needed” basis by the Steering Committee of the CGO. 2. The Steering Committee of the CGO will be composed of one member of the NPC, who shall chair the Steering Committee, up to ten current or former chapter HGOs selected by the NPC, and a representative of the YDSA Chapter Health and Intersectionality Committee Other members of the NPC may act as non-voting liaisons. The Steering Committee may recommend candidates for addition to the Steering Committee to the NPC. 3. The CGO Steering Committee may draft and pass bylaws to govern its work and may, at its discretion, create subcommittees to carry out its work. 4. The CGO will: 1. Determine appropriate training requirements for HGOs. 2. Organize meetings open to all DSA members interested in the grievance process, which may include skillshares, training, and breakout sessions for consultation and mutual support of chapter HGOs. 3. Seek input from chapter HGOs about existing community accountability and mediation programs, and will provide support to chapter HGOs in developing and implementing such programs. 4. Develop materials to assist chapter HGOs and, with the assistance of the National Tech Committee (NTC), work to ensure that materials related to the grievance process are accessible by members on the DSA website. Said materials will include template forms for reporting and responding to complaints and appeals. 5. Assist the NGP chairs in conducting an annual survey of chapter HGOs in December of each year. 6. Review this policy from time to time and draft proposed revisions as necessary. 5. The CGO chair will: 1. Work to develop the HGO community by facilitating opportunities and a space for HGOs to discuss chapter situations, seek support and feedback, and review plans of action. 2. Collaborate with the NGP on training for HGOs. 3. With the NGP chairs, maintain a list of chapter HGOs. 4. Identify and work to develop HGOs in chapters without identified HGOs. 1. National Grievance Panel. The National Grievance Panel (“NGP”) consists of DSA’s national HGOs. The NGP will investigate national complaints and appeals and make recommendations on complaints and appeals to the NPC. 1. The NGP will consist of a panel of members appointed by the NPC. The NGP will be chaired by two co-chairs, selected from its membership by the NPC. 1. NGP members will be appointed for two years and will be appointed the January following an NPC election. Additional members may be appointed by the NPC upon recommendation from the NGP chairs. 2. The roster of all NGP members will be available to DSA members, but which members may be assigned to individual cases will only be known to the chair, the NPC, and other panel members. 3. Members will be appointed or removed from the NGP only with a supermajority of NPC (12 votes). 4. Members of the NGP will recuse themselves from any matter under this policy in which they have a conflict of interest, or in which a conflict of interest is likely to arise. No NGP member will review a matter originating from their local chapter. 2. The NGP will: 1. Serve as HGOs at the national level. 2. Review appeals to the NPC in accordance with this policy. 3. Investigate complaints made to the NPC in accordance with this policy. 4. Review requests for national expulsion made to the NPC in accordance with this policy. 5. Identify complaints and appeals which may require guidance from legal counsel. 6. Strive for consistency in practice in applying DSA grievance procedures, policies, and provide support for chapters to support chapter-level consistency with those same provisions. 7. Prepare a report for Convention on the grievance process, up to and including recommendations for revisions. 3. The NGP chairs will: 1. Monitor the national grievance email address and respond to queries, concerns, complaints, and any other matters, serving as the first point of contact for complaints and appeals at the national level. The NGP chairs will maintain a national grievance submission and appeal systems, and monitor a national grievance email to accept appeals and receive complaints. 2. Track the status of national grievances or appeals, triaging grievances/appeals, compiling finalized NGP investigations to present to the NPC, delivering notice of NPC case adjudications to all involved parties, and collecting grievance reports from chapters. 3. Lead and coordinate meetings of NGP members at minimum monthly. 4. Assign and manage members of the NGP to investigate complaints made to the NPC and to consider appeals under this policy. 5. Conduct a review of each case finalized by NGP members before NPC review to ensure consistency in practice and recommended resolutions. 6. Maintain records of complaints, investigations, expelled members, and other relevant information regarding membership status. 7. Develop standardized forms for reports, investigations, and procedural recommendations for use by NGP members. 8. In conjunction with the CGO, provide for training of NGP members and HGOs in best practices, conflict resolution, investigations, mediation, and other practices. 9. Collaborate with the CGO in the creation of a survey for chapter HGOs, covering reports of harassment, code of conduct violations, and areas that chapters identified need more support from the NGP, CGO, or national DSA to fulfill their obligations under this policy. 6. Local Structures. 1. Each DSA chapter will: 1. Have at least one member designated as harassment/grievance officer(s) (“HGO”), who may be elected by membership or appointed by the chapter steering committee, at the chapter’s discretion. HGOs may not simultaneously be members of the chapter’s Steering Committee. 2. Chapters with more than one hundred members will have at least two HGOs. 3. Determine term limits for chapter HGOs and develop methods for removing HGOs for cause. 4. Establish and monitor an email address to function as a confidential reporting “hotline” that is only accessible by the HGOs. 5. Maintain forms both for reporting and responding to complaints and grievance appeals. 6. Determine which HGO(s) will be responsible for each complaint that comes to its attention. 2. A chapter’s Steering Committee will have sole authority to adjudicate complaints that may come before it as described in this policy. This will not be construed to abrogate the authority of the NPC as the highest decision making body of DSA between conventions. 3. Chapters may pass local codes of conduct in accordance with their chapter bylaws. 4. Unless a chapter’s bylaws state otherwise, the chapter’s Steering Committee will make determinations of member discipline under this policy. 5. Chapters will provide the names and email addresses for the HGOs to the National Grievance Coordinator and the Committee of Grievance Officers on an annual basis. 6. Chapter HGOs and Chapter Steering Committee Members will recuse themselves from any matter under this policy in which they have a conflict of interest, or in which a conflict of interest is likely to arise. 7. If a chapter receives a complaint and all HGOs recuse themselves from the matter, the Steering Committee will appoint a member to serve as HGO to address that complaint. 7. Grievances. 1. Complaints. Any member that has been harassed by another member or believes another member’s conduct violates an applicable code of conduct or their chapter’s bylaws may make a complaint about the conduct of the other member to a chapter HGO. 1. A complaint arising from online behavior of a member made by a member of a separate chapter may be made either to the accused member’s chapter HGOs or to the NPC. 2. Chapter HGOs will maintain and monitor an email address accessible only to the HGOs to receive complaints and other communications regarding complaints. 3. The National Grievance Coordinator and NGP will maintain and monitor an email address accessible only to the National Grievance Coordinator and NGP co-chairs to receive complaints to the NPC or other national communications regarding complaints. 4. Complaints will be made in writing, preferably to the applicable HGO email address. 5. There is no time limit for making a complaint. 6. Except as provided in subsection i of this section, if a member contacts the National Grievance Coordinator, the NGP, or the NPC regarding a complaint without first having had the matter adjudicated at the local level, their complaint will be referred to the local chapter. Not having a chapter HGO will not be considered a reason for the NGP and/or NPC to agree to accept a complaint. 2. Disciplinary Referrals. Where a member has allegedly violated this policy, any applicable member code of conduct, or other authority, a Steering Committee or HGO may issue a disciplinary referral against a member, which will be made in the same manner as a complaint and will be treated as a complaint under this policy. 3. Preliminary Procedures. 1. Upon receipt of a complaint, the responsible HGO(s) will provide notice of the complaint to the accused member within a reasonable time, ideally within seven (7) days of receiving the complaint. Notice will include either a copy of the complaint or a summary which includes the specific conduct alleged to have violated this policy, an applicable code of conduct, or other authority. 2. At any time following the receipt of a complaint, an HGO may notify the Steering Committee of the complaint and request from the Steering Committee temporary discipline as necessary to protect the health and safety of members and the integrity of the organization. 3. An HGO may recommend that a complaining member and an accused member do not communicate with each other or with specific other persons for the duration of the grievance process. 4. With consent of the complaining member and the accused member, an HGO may refer a matter for alternative dispute resolution where appropriate. 5. Once notified, the accused member will have seven (7) days to respond to the complaint. If the accused member requests additional time to respond, it should be freely given, but in no circumstances will the accused member be given more than fourteen (14) days to respond unless extraordinary circumstances justify the delay. 6. If an accused member fails to timely respond or request additional time, the HGO will recommend the Steering Committee take appropriate disciplinary action. 7. If an accused party denies the substance of the complaint, the HGO will conduct an investigation under Section 7(d) of this policy. 8. At any stage of a process under this policy, an accused member may name another member as an advisor or support person, provided the named member agrees to serve as advisor or support person. The advisor or support person may be any member who is not otherwise a party involved in the incident or a witness to the conduct stated in the complaint. 1. The advisor or support person’s role is to provide guidance and/or emotional support, and may not speak on behalf of a member or disrupt any meeting or proceedings in any manner. 2. Advisors or support persons may be excluded from participation if they fail to adhere to restrictions outlined here. 3. Conduct by an advisor or support person which constitutes retaliation under Section 11 of this policy will be the subject of a separate complaint under this policy. 4. Investigation. An HGO may investigate a complaint by interviewing people with direct knowledge of the substance of the complaint, requesting appropriate documentation from the complaining member, accused member, or other person in possession of relevant documents or by any and all other necessary means. 1. An HGO will complete the investigation in a reasonable time, ideally within ten (10) days of receiving the accused member’s written response. 5. Report. Following investigation, the HGO will create a report determining whether the complaint is credible, whether the alleged conduct violates this policy, and whether the alleged conduct more likely than not occurred. 1. Grievance reports are confidential and will not be disseminated outside of the HGOs, the Steering Committee, the complaining member, and the accused member. 2. A report may contain disciplinary recommendations to the Steering Committee. 3. Reports will be transmitted to the Steering Committee, the complaining member, and the accused member in a timely fashion. Grievance reports are ideally transmitted within thirty (30) days of the complaint being filed. If an HGO requires more than sixty (60) days to complete the report, the HGO must communicate the need for additional time to the Steering Committee, the complaining member, and the accused member. 6. Adjudication. The Steering Committee has sole decision making authority as to whether conduct more likely than not occurred and whether conduct violated this policy. The Steering Committee has authority to determine matters of member discipline under this policy, in accordance with any applicable bylaws. 1. The Steering Committee will follow processes described in the chapter bylaws in adjudicating a complaint, provided those bylaws provisions do not contradict this policy. 2. Each complaint will be assessed on a case-by-case basis by the Steering Committee 3. To adjudicate a complaint, the Steering Committee will determine: 1. Whether the alleged conduct more likely than not occurred; 2. Whether the conduct violated this policy or an applicable chapter policy; and, 3. Whether the accused member’s conduct warrants discipline. 4. The Steering Committee will make all necessary decisions on complaints in a timely fashion, not to exceed thirty (30) days from the receipt of the HGO’s report. 5. The Steering Committee will not delegate its decision on adjudications or discipline to any committee, subcommittee, or person; provided, however, that a chapter’s bylaws may require certain disciplinary matters to be considered by a chapter meeting. 6. The adjudication of a grievance will be in writing, and will contain findings based on the HGO report and any other evidence considered by the Steering Committee. 7. The Steering Committee will notify the complaining member, the accused member, and the HGOs of any adjudication and of the right to an appeal within three (3) days of a decision. This communication will include a copy of the written adjudication. 8. Discipline. 1. The Steering Committee has authority to issue both temporary and final remedies during any processes under this policy. Chapters also have authority to issue final remedies during processes under this policy according to their bylaws. 2. Temporary Discipline. Upon notice of a complaint to the Steering Committee by an HGO, at request of the HGO or on its own, the Steering Committee may issue a temporary remedy as necessary to protect the health and welfare of members and the integrity of the organization. 1. No temporary discipline will continue beyond the adjudication of the complaint. 2. No temporary discipline will continue beyond one hundred and twenty (120) days from the date the member was notified of the temporary discipline, unless extended by the NPC. 3. Nothing in this policy should be construed to limit the Steering Committee from removing members from online spaces as temporary discipline. The Steering Committee may delegate the authority to remove members from online spaces to moderators at its discretion. 3. Final Discipline. A final remedy will only be issued following adjudication of the complaint where the Steering Committee determines that the conduct more likely than not occurred, that the conduct violated this policy or an applicable chapter policy, and that the accused member’s conduct warrants discipline. 1. If a local chapter has established suspension or expulsion procedures, the Steering Committee is authorized to enforce these remedies and penalties in accordance with those procedures. 2. If the local chapter does not have established suspension or expulsion procedures, they will adopt the procedures outlined in Article III, Section 4 of the DSA Constitution and Article I, Section 3 of DSA bylaws, substituting the NPC majority required with a Steering Committee majority. 4. Determinations. In determining temporary or final discipline, the following will be considered: 1. The request of the complaining member. 2. The facts of the case and the severity of the offense. 3. The response of the accused member. 4. Any history of relevant behavior by the accused member. 5. The recommendation of the HGO. 5. Time. All decisions regarding member discipline determined by the Steering Committee will be made within thirty (30) days of the receipt of the HGO’s report. Determinations of member discipline by a chapter meeting, where permitted or required by a chapter’s bylaws, will be made within forty-five (45) days of the receipt of the report at a special meeting called specifically for that purpose. 6. Remedies. Remedies may include: 1. A formal discussion between the disciplined member and the Steering Committee to develop a plan to change the offending behavior(s). 2. Censure of the disciplined member. 3. Suspension from committee meetings and other organizational events. 4. Removal from committees. 5. Removal from shared resources or communications platforms. 6. Suspension from DSA. 1. No suspension from a DSA will be effective for a period longer than three (3) years. 2. A member’s suspension may contain conditions for re-integration at the end of the suspension period. 7. Expulsion from DSA. 1. Expulsion from a chapter is treated immediately as a full suspension and immediately forwarded up to the NGP to begin the national expulsion process.. 2. NGP will review the expulsion notes and proceedings to ensure expulsions are for conduct and not politically related expulsions before forwarding to the NPC. The NPC will address requests for national expulsion as a complaint under this policy. 3. A nationally expelled member may petition to return to DSA after five (5) years have passed from the date of initial expulsion. All petitions to return to DSA will be made to the NPC. 8. Any combination of remedies deemed appropriate. 9. Any and all other relief deemed necessary and just by the Steering Committee or the chapter. 9. Appeals. 1. Right to Appeal. A complaining member, an accused member, or a chapter HGO may appeal a chapter Steering Committee’s adjudication to the NPC. An adjudication by the NPC may not be appealed. 2. Appeal of Temporary Discipline. Temporary discipline pending the outcome of a grievance decision is not appealable until the final adjudication of the complaint or the expiration of one hundred twenty (120) days from the date the member was notified of the temporary discipline, whichever is sooner. 3. Grounds. The limited grounds for appeal are: 1. The behavior did not violate this policy. 2. Procedural errors, misconduct, or conflicts of interest affected the fairness of the outcome. Error that did not affect the fairness of the outcome will not warrant the overturning of an adjudication. 3. The discipline determined by Steering was grossly disproportionate to the conduct. 4. Time. There is no specific time limit for the filing of an appeal; however, the NPC may choose to reject as moot an appeal which does not have an ongoing impact on a member’s status. 5. Form. An appeal to the NPC will be initiated by contacting the National Grievance Coordinator, who will provide the party with the appropriate appeal forms, which will then be referred to the NGP. 6. Determination. The NPC has sole and ultimate decision-making authority on all appeals. The NGP may assist the NPC in reviewing grievance appeals and making recommendations to the NPC. Decisions of the NPC are not appealable. 7. Remedies. The NPC may affirm or reverse a chapter Steering Committee’s adjudication and/or a chapter Steering Committee’s decision on member discipline, in whole or in part. Chapters are bound by the NPC’s decision on an appeal. The NPC may also choose to remand an appeal to the chapter for further action. Upon remand, chapters are obligated to follow the recommendations of the NPC. 10. Confidentiality. 1. General Policy. The grievance process under this policy is confidential. However, DSA leaders can often find themselves in difficult situations where they are trying to build trust with their comrades through transparency, but are fearful of disclosing private information. DSA leadership and HGOs will follow this guidance to protect the confidentiality of members: 1. A complaining member will not be silenced. HGOs can explain that maintaining confidentiality may help expedite the investigation, preserve the integrity of the process, and de-escalate conflict. A complaining member who agrees to confidentiality should understand that the confidentiality request is only for the period of the investigation. 2. Accused members will not be punished for making a good-faith effort to produce evidence for the consideration of HGOs and/or the Steering Committee. Communications regarding a complaint that violate any temporary discipline of a member and/or an HGO’s recommendations under Section 7(c)(iii) of this policy (if any) will not be considered as being in good-faith. 3. Accused members will not be punished for seeking advice or emotional support from a person they designate as an advisor or support person under this policy. 4. Anyone involved in the investigation, including the complaining member and the accused member, must understand that disclosure of information regarding the complaint can escalate conflict. Escalation of conflict by a complaining member, an accused member, or a third-party may constitute retaliation under this policy. 5. HGOs and chapter leaders will refrain from conveying any information provided to them in confidence without the express permission of the party who gave them that information, except as necessary to effect the adjudication of the complaint. 6. Chapters and Steering Committees will keep grievance deliberations confidential and discuss such matters only in executive session. All votes must be a matter of record. 7. In order to prevent additional harm and/or the spreading of misinformation, chapter leaders will work with the NGP before releasing information about a complaint at the chapter level. A chapter is not in any way restricted from confirming or denying a person’s membership status to members. 8. The NPC, National Grievance Coordinator, and NGP will abide by these confidentiality requirements. 9. Chapter leadership and HGOs will work through the National Grievance Coordinator and the NGP and not contact the NPC directly about grievance matters. Chapters and/or parties are not permitted to “lobby” the NPC about their desired outcome on appeal, and efforts to do so may be considered retaliation. 10. When the Steering Committee has adjudicated a grievance matter, the ruling will be privately conveyed to the parties in a manner that ensures the safety of survivors and fairness to the accused. 2. The National Grievance Coordinator and staff responsible for maintaining membership records will maintain a list of expelled members. A chapter may inquire if a specific individual has been expelled and is ineligible for membership, and the National Grievance Coordinator or National staff will ONLY confirm or deny that specific individual’s presence on the list. Requests for additional information may be made to the NPC through the NGP. Chapters will not be provided access to additional information regarding expelled members unless the NPC determines that a particular chapter request merits an exception. 3. No confidential grievance information will be disclosed to law enforcement or any party to a civil lawsuit without a valid and enforceable subpoena requesting said information. Any HGO or chapter receiving a subpoena or informal request for information or evidence from anyone outside of the parties or in relation to any legal, judicial, administrative or other kind of action should contact the National Grievance Coordinator immediately. 11. Retaliation. 1. Retaliation prohibited. Retaliation for making a complaint or assisting a member in making a complaint under this policy is prohibited. Retaliation against HGOs for investigating and reporting complaints is prohibited. Retaliation against Steering Committee members for adjudicating complaints and/or making decisions on member discipline is prohibited. 2. If any party to the complaint, HGO, or Steering Committee member believes there has been retaliation, they should inform the HGO, who will treat the allegation of retaliatory conduct as a separate complaint under this policy. 3. The following behaviors may be considered retaliatory and will be considered the subject of a new complaint involving any person(s) engaged in retaliatory conduct: 1. Intentionally exposing confidential information outside of the grievance process in a manner calculated to target the complaining member, the accused member and/or other individuals involved in the process. 2. Filing complaints under this policy in bad faith with no merit against individuals they want to be suspended or expelled for political or personal reasons, or to invoke confidentiality where none is warranted. 3. Organizing to avoid accountability among friends, supporters, and others inside and outside DSA to foster support and degenerate the grievance process and/or to enlist support from outside organizations. 4. Publicly disparaging a complaining member or others involved in the investigation by directly and/or indirectly targeting participants with profanity, slurs, or other language prohibited by this policy. 5. Vigilantism/self-help measures that include public shaming, contacting employers, community groups, family members, and romantic/relationship partners, and other harmful public actions. 6. Escalation of conflict while the grievance is pending by using social media, personal contacts, publications, organizing efforts, social networks, or any other way that results in an escalation of the conflict. 7. Manipulating chapter election processes to unfairly prevent parties involved in grievances from assuming leadership positions. 8. Failing to reveal a conflict of interest or failure to recuse by those involved in investigation or decision-making with regard to a complaint, including HGOs who do not reveal actual conflicts of interest and/or do not recuse themselves from matters where such a conflict is likely to arise. 9. Taking other adverse action against those involved in the process, including piling on additional work for people in leadership positions to make them look bad, and subjecting them to continuing retaliation as described above for the way they conducted the investigation and/or decisions which impacted the grievance outcome. 4. Retaliation reported during the grievance process is treated as a separate complaint, but evidence of retaliatory conduct may be considered by the NPC as part of any decision on appeal.. 5. Refusal by the chapter to implement a final appeal ruling may be considered retaliation. The NPC may also take action against chapter leadership to ensure its decisions are honored. 12. Alternative Dispute Resolution. 1. Use of Alternative Dispute Resolution. In certain circumstances, an alternative dispute resolution based on restorative practices and the principles of transformative justice may be preferable to a formal investigation and adjudication of a complaint. Where the complaining member and accused member agree and the HGO determines there is no risk of further harm from communication between the parties, an HGO may recommend that the complaint be referred for alternative dispute resolution under this section. 2. Nothing in this policy should be construed as limiting the use of Alternative Dispute Resolution or other informal practices to resolve conflict where no complaint has been filed. 3. Chapters will work to ensure that local bylaws, codes of conduct, and policies permit restorative practices, mediation, and/or other transformative remedies. 4. All alternative dispute resolution is voluntary and no alternative dispute resolution may be imposed upon the parties. 5. Alternative dispute resolution will only be used where the complaining member is demonstrably comfortable with that approach and the accused member is ready to acknowledge responsibility for the harm caused. 6. Alternative dispute resolution may include: 1. Mediation. 2. Talking or Discussion Circles. 3. Requesting a training from national committees 4. Other restorative practices. 7. Any information shared as part of an alternative dispute resolution is subject to the same confidentiality as information shared during an investigation. 8. An HGO will report the outcome of any alternative dispute resolution to the Steering Committee, whether successful or unsuccessful. 9. If an HGO refers a matter for alternative dispute resolution and the resolution is unsuccessful, the HGO will investigate according to the terms of this policy and make the appropriate report to the Steering Committee. 13. Political Discipline 1. Expulsion of a member under the above policies and processes constitutes a “conduct expulsion,” or a finding that the member engaged in “undemocratic, disruptive behavior,” permitting expulsion under the second criterion of Article I, Section 3 of DSA’s Bylaws. 2. A “political expulsion” is defined as an expulsion on the basis of the first criterion of Article I, Section 3 of DSA’s Bylaws, “substantial disagreement with the principles or policies of the organization.” 3. With the exception of Article 13, no article of this policy applies to political expulsions or to any other disciplinary processes for which the subject is the political rather than personal conduct of the accused. 4. With the exception of Article 13, this policy may not be used to adjudicate a political expulsion, nor may it be used to apply other discipline to a member on the basis of political disagreement or otherwise adjudicate political disagreement between DSA members. 5. DSA’s political decision-making bodies, namely the National Political Committee, chapter Steering Committees, chapter general bodies, and the National Convention, have sole authority over political expulsions. 1. A member expelled on political grounds may appeal their expulsion. Political expulsion by a chapter Steering Committee may be appealed to the chapter general body. Political expulsion by a chapter general body may be appealed to the National Political Committee. Political expulsion by the National Political Committee may be appealed to the National Convention. 2. Members facing political expulsion must receive specific written notice of the charges against them and must be given the opportunity to be heard before the body responsible for adjudicating the charges. 3. HGOs and bodies which are primarily responsible for components of the grievance process, such as the NGP and CGO, have no role in the investigation or adjudication of a member’s political conduct. 6. There is a general policy of transparency for all political disciplinary processes. The pertinent political information used to justify any political expulsion must be disclosed to the general membership. Status: Adopted Summary Members of DSA may be expelled for undemocratic or disruptive conduct or for substantial political disagreement with DSA. While rare, expulsion on the basis of political disagreement should be transparent to membership. Full text Preamble: A member of DSA may be expelled for one of two primary reasons: poor conduct, or substantial political disagreement with DSA. Expulsion on the basis of the former criterion is a conduct expulsion, and expulsion on the basis of the latter criterion is a political expulsion. In cases of expulsion on the basis of conduct, there is a general policy of confidentiality and privacy for the involved parties, which prohibits DSA mediators, grievance officers, or elected leadership from publicly discussing or disclosing details of the grievance in question which are not otherwise publicly available without the permission of all involved parties. In cases of expulsion on the basis of political disagreement, there is a general policy of transparency, which requires DSA’s elected leadership to disclose to the general membership the pertinent political information used to justify the expulsion. As long as membership in a self-described democratic centralist organization is considered a legitimate basis for expulsion by the DSA Constitution and Bylaws, expulsion on this basis is considered to be a political expulsion, and is subject to the same transparency requirements as expulsion on the basis of political disagreement. Expulsion on either basis is not intended as a general purpose tool to resolve disagreement. Political expulsions are under the sole purview of DSA’s elected political leadership, and the DSA grievance process is not intended to be used to adjudicate political disputes between members. Effective text: Therefore, be it resolved, the preamble and Article 1a of CR08: Unified Grievance Policy, are amended as follows, with additions green and underlined, deletions red and struck out, and omitted text unaffected: UNIFORM GRIEVANCE POLICY Democratic Socialists of America is committed to creating a space that is welcoming and inclusive to members of all genders, races, and classes. The following policy provides guidelines to ensure that everyone is able to organize without fear of harassment, abuse, or harm. We further recognize that interpersonal conflict can arise within our organization and manifest itself within and without our political processes. The processes created by this policy are designed not only to address harassing conduct, but also conduct that may interfere with our core political work to address inappropriate personal conduct by members, and not political conduct which may nevertheless interfere with DSA's core political work. 1. General Provisions 1. Any investigation or proceeding by any DSA body, including but not limited to a chapter, a chapter steering committee (“SC”), or the National Political Committee (“NPC”), which may result in a member being disciplined by the organization on the basis of their personal conduct, whether permanently, temporarily, or otherwise, must follow the procedures laid out in this policy. Be it finally resolved, that CR08 is further amended to add a new Article 13, to immediately follow the existing Article 12: 13. Political Discipline 1. Expulsion of a member under the above policies and processes constitutes a “conduct expulsion,” or a finding that the member engaged in “undemocratic, disruptive behavior,” permitting expulsion under the second criterion of Article I, Section 3 of DSA’s Bylaws. 2. A “political expulsion” is defined as an expulsion on the basis of the first criterion of Article I, Section 3 of DSA’s Bylaws, “substantial disagreement with the principles or policies of the organization.” 3. With the exception of Article 13, no article of this policy applies to political expulsions or to any other disciplinary processes for which the subject is the political rather than personal conduct of the accused. 4. With the exception of Article 13, this policy may not be used to adjudicate a political expulsion, nor may it be used to apply other discipline to a member on the basis of political disagreement or otherwise adjudicate political disagreement between DSA members. 5. DSA’s political decision-making bodies, namely the National Political Committee, chapter Steering Committees, chapter general bodies, and the National Convention, have sole authority over political expulsions. 1. A member expelled on political grounds may appeal their expulsion. Political expulsion by a chapter Steering Committee may be appealed to the chapter general body. Political expulsion by a chapter general body may be appealed to the National Political Committee. Political expulsion by the National Political Committee may be appealed to the National Convention. 2. Members facing political expulsion must receive specific written notice of the charges against them and must be given the opportunity to be heard before the body responsible for adjudicating the charges. 3. HGOs and bodies which are primarily responsible for components of the grievance process, such as the NGP and CGO, have no role in the investigation or adjudication of a member’s political conduct. 6. There is a general policy of transparency for all political disciplinary processes. The pertinent political information used to justify any political expulsion must be disclosed to the general membership. Full text WHEREAS, the 2023 DSA National Convention mandated the creation of what came to be known as the Trans Rights and Bodily Autonomy Campaign Commission (TRBA). WHEREAS, the NPC Implementation Resolution which created TRBA states that the TRBA Steering Committee shall “draft a resolution for the 2025 DSA convention outlining either a rationale and plan for its reauthorization or a rationale and plan for its dissolution”. WHEREAS, TRBA’s initial mandate was largely made up of short-term goals, which TRBA quickly fulfilled by holding a successful Kickoff Mass Call and a Day of Action on Trans Day of Visibility 2024 with dozens of chapters across the country participating. WHEREAS, over two dozen chapters have run campaigns based off of TRBA’s Trans Sanctuary City Toolkit in the past two years, successfully passing Trans Sanctuary Resolutions in jurisdictions such as but not limited to Ithaca, NY; Columbia, MO; Sacramento, CA; Akron, OH; Dallas County, TX; and Washington DC, cumulatively covering several million people. WHEREAS, DSA chapters such as but not limited to Los Angeles, Metro DC, Chicago, and New York City have carried out pressure campaigns against academic medical centers that caved to the Trump administration by suspending pediatric gender-affirming care. WHEREAS, TRBA has outgrown its 2023 mandate and chapters have embarked on extensive trans and abortion rights campaigns, intervening in state legislative fights across the country, stopping anti-trans bills and passing landmark trans rights legislation such as the Kelly Loving Act in Colorado, and trans and abortion rights campaigns are now the most common legislative work for DSA chapters. WHEREAS, the TRBA Steering Committee has seen significant turnover as leaders have been torn between their local campaigns in this issue area and their national work. While growing leadership from trans people leading campaigns in this area has been a political benefit for TRBA, the consistent bottlenecks in the function of the national body have been operational capacity for tracking chapter campaigns, promotion and turnout for mass calls, interfacing with DSA’s org tools, and other day-to-day operations work, leading to diminished campaigns capacity for a national body facilitating work between dozens of chapters and nearly nonexistent capacity to participate in any national legislative processes. WHEREAS, the Republican Party’s fascist assault on trans life, carried out through the vector of state power and regulations, is not only an existential threat to trans people but also represents an attack on the broader working class’ capacity for solidarity, and Democratic Socialists of America is uniquely positioned to fight for trans liberation as a grassroots organization with hundreds of elected officials, a network of labor militants, and an extremely high proportion of trans leaders. THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the Trans Rights and Bodily Autonomy Campaign Commission (TRBA) be renewed through the 2027 DSA National Convention with a new mandate of: 1. Being an organizing hub for trans rights and bodily autonomy campaigns in the organization, with a primary focus on legislative campaigns, by stitching together chapter campaigns into a national strategic framework. 2. Providing toolkits, resources, and mentorship to support chapters in their trans rights and bodily autonomy campaigns. 3. Collaborating with other DSA national bodies (e.g. National Labor Commission, National Electoral Commission) when overlap in organizing work necessitates it. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that members of TRBA will take on the responsibilities listed below, helping to alleviate capacity issues: 1. Aiding chapters in creating and carrying-out trans rights and bodily autonomy campaigns, with a primary focus on legislation. 2. Administering the TRBA field budget and matching-funds programs at the direction of the Steering Committee. 3. Maintaining central informational resources such as TRBA’s Legislative Index in coordination with the Steering Committee and Commission members to monitor the activities of state and federal legislatures and agencies. 4. Help TRBA monitor and intervene in national legislative and administrative actions and in resisting the Trump administration. 5. Running legislative campaigns and civics trainings and helping chapters intervene in the legislative process, with a focus on trans rights and bodily autonomy. BE IT FINALLY RESOLVED, that the TRBA Steering Committee shall, 60 days after Convention adjournment, hold elections for the 2025-27 TRBA Steering Committee according to the following criteria for voter eligibility: 1. Has applied to the TRBA national body within 30 days of Convention adjournment. 2. Has substantively engaged in organizing a local, state, or national TRBA campaign in the past two years, to be attested along with specification of said campaign(s) in a form sent to all existing applicants to the TRBA national body and made available on trba.dsausa.org within 30 days of convention adjournment. Full text WHEREAS, since the 2023 convention adopted the last consensus resolution drafted by the National Labor Commission, the uptick in labor action has continued and spread. We are proud to say we have begun executing several of the actions laid out in that document and intend to continue the work that it laid out in the years to come. WHEREAS, the National Labor Commission was renewed in the 2023 DSA Convention. WHEREAS, since the 2023 Convention, the National Labor Commission has continued to support labor work within chapters and through national campaigns. WHEREAS, the COVID-19 pandemic transformed the terrain we organize on. While many of these effects were negative, the mass adoption of key digital tools and the necessity of organizing to survive triggered an uptick in labor activity that has continued in the years since. WHEREAS, the international ruling class continues to grow its power and increasingly threatens the sovereignty of democratically elected governments and international structures. While commerce operates in a global system, workers are constrained by borders and laws that in many cases punish rather than protect them. WHEREAS, the climate crisis is escalating rapidly and organized workers are the agent of change that can transform our world. WHEREAS, the current US Presidential administration has made a priority of dismantling essential structures that serve its populous and specifically targeted unionized workers who provide these services. Furthermore, the rightward shift within the NLRB means workers and unions cannot rely on friendly rulings and processes, the labor movement must continue to focus on shop-floor power and struggle. WHEREAS, US unions in large part failed to seize on the opportunities that arose in the past five years including a friendly NLRB, a tight labor market and uptick in militancy on the shop floor. In many cases these unions sit on large sums of money that can and must be used to grow the labor movement. Forcing these unions into motion will take organized effort from the rank and file. WHEREAS, some unions, mostly those with a more robust internal democracy, have seized on the opportunities of the moment, engaging in aggressive, militant, member-driven contract and new organizing campaigns, most notably the UAW’s Stand Up Strike in the fall of 2023. WHEREAS, at the conclusion of that strike, UAW President Shawn Fain called for mass worker action around May Day 2028 and lined up the Big 3 Automaker contracts to expire on that date and called on other unionists to line up their contracts to end that date, a call that has resonated through the broader working class. WHEREAS, DSA has modeled what it looks like to empower workers to organize and lead in their unions and workplaces. Through its joint project with UE, the Emergency Workplace Organizing Committee has aided the formation of dozens of new union shops. Through its solidarity work during key strikes at the Big Three Automakers, the University of California System, Starbucks and more it has enabled workers in struggle to remain on the line one day longer and stronger. Through its ongoing work educating and connecting members to further their organizing and their political analysis it has helped to cohere a movement of socialists focused on transforming the labor movement. WHEREAS, as instructed by the last convention DSA Labor has begun the process of standing up local EWOC formations and a national salt training program. Through local EWOCs and the “Workers Organizing Workers” training series we are building our repertoire and capacity to train worker organizers on essential skills that will contribute to their short term projects and long term capacity for shop floor organizing. WHEREAS, Reform movements in major unions have continued to be an important part of our political project but one in which we have only engaged thus far in unofficial individual capacities. WHEREAS, militant workers have used non-reformist labor reforms to accelerate their growing their power on the shopfloor and - despite the non-passage of the PRO Act - organizing workers and DSA members across the country are campaigning for state and local policy changes that can help grow the power of workers vis-a-vis the ruling class. WHEREAS, DSA is currently the largest socialist organization in the country and intends to continue growing and developing toward representation of the working class as a whole. Our mission remains the development of organizing skills amongst worker leaders, the building of democratic structures in the workplace, and ultimately the establishment of democratic socialism in our lifetimes. WHEREAS the dismantling of federal agencies, the firing of civilian federal workers, and the elimination of collective bargaining rights for almost a million federal workers represent significant attacks on the working class’s public services and the democratic rights of all workers to organize that socialists have the strongest interest in defending, and WHEREAS the NPC adopted a resolution encouraging chapters to act in solidarity with the Federal Unionists Network, and several chapters have prioritized campaigns in solidarity with the federal workers, including East Bay and Metro Detroit, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that this convention commits to continue its work of uniting the socialist and labor movements with the near term goal of turning May Day 2028 into a demonstration of bottom up worker power. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that in in the years to come the National Labor Commission will continue our efforts around the following areas of work: 1. Connecting current union members in our ranks and encouraging their organizing on the shop floor Socialism’s true home is in the workplace and in the labor movement. In order to overcome the historic divide between the socialist and labor movements in this country, DSA must continue to reconnect the two at the level of the rank and file. DSA recommits to the Rank and File Strategy that has led our successful labor work for the last 6 years. DSA will continue to encourage its comrades to take jobs in unionized workplaces for the long haul, and will continue to prioritize recruiting existing shop floor leaders into DSA. Comrades that work together should organize to build solidarity, win material gains for themselves and their coworkers, oppose all forms of oppression in the workplace, and build a more militant, democratic labor movement. The National Labor Commission will continue to prioritize building relationships with rank-and-file union members, including providing them resources for bottom up organizing and supporting them in efforts to run for union leadership. Additionally the NLC will encourage the organic development of DSA industrial networks and will continue supporting members’ attendance at the biannual Labor Notes Conference and local Troublemakers Schools. We will encourage chapter labor formations to serve as a home for DSA members organizing in their workplace, both in bringing together the broader socialist movement to support them in their organizing and in being a place they can bring their coworkers to introduce them to DSA and the socialist movement. The NLC will continue toward previously stated goals of 1) developing an organization more deeply rooted in the organized segment of the multi-racial US working class, 2) developing a cadre of dedicated socialist organizers rooted in the workplace, and 3) winning more workers to the cause of democratic socialism. 2. Promoting Salting and New Shop Organizing DSA will continue to encourage members and supporters to take jobs in strategic not-yet-union workplaces where they can support and lead campaigns to win union recognition and collective bargaining rights. Through EWOC and the Workers Organizing Workers program, we will train the next generation of shop floor militants through hands-on training led by experienced volunteer organizers. DSA will provide the necessary resources to ensure the DSA Labor “Workers Organizing Workers” training program can continue to recruit salts, conduct its quarterly trainings, support organizers with mentorship and political education, and expand to meet the growing need for knowledgeable shop floor leaders. 3. Spreading Our Politics Through Solidarity Actions DSA has taken significant steps toward transforming the image that workers on strike have of socialists on their picket line. Through our approach of leading with material support and following up with relationship building we have forged strong bonds between our members and a wide array of worker leaders. This has been made possible by the continued gathering of our members to share tactics as well as our Labor Solidarity Fund. In order to provide even more support directly to workers as well as chapters who are engaging in solidarity work, DSA will commit to growing the Solidarity Fund through national fundraising efforts, as well as giving chapters the tools and training to fundraise locally. We will also expand the scope of the fund to allow it to provide for the needs that militant organizers require beyond direct service. The Solidarity Captains’ Network will continue to build structures to enable every DSA chapter to support workers in motion, by developing leaders, providing trainings, and equipping DSA with the means to support emerging labor struggles. 4. Organizing Amazon In 2023 we committed to prioritizing logistics organizing and saw the power that came from workers at UPS hubs across the country coming together to threaten a nationwide strike. In 2024 the National Labor Commission voted to shift our focus to the logistics giant Amazon. Through our #OrganizeAmazon campaign we are honing in on the new organizing taking place among Amazon warehouse workers and delivery drivers and continuing to build a strong, active network of shop floor militants. 5. Seizing the May Day 2028 Moment The UAW call for a May Day 2028 general strike is ambitious and aspirational - and DSA recognizes the organizing in the lead up to the date as a potential breakthrough for our class. The UAW and other unions have the goal of aligning a range of contracts in the months surrounding May 1. DSA committed to organizing with rank and file activists across unions in cities across the country to build connections and strategy in the lead up to May Day 2028. We will ally with a range of unions and organizations to create a plan for moving towards 2028 with actions, events, and ongoing organizing in 2026 and 2027. The NLC, along with the NPC, shall anchor DSA efforts to build towards 2028. 6. Developing a concrete program to advance union democracy While we have made significant progress on many of the tasks we laid out in 2023, our union democracy efforts were in large part put on the back burner. This year we renew our commitment to building militant, class-struggle unions. We also re-affirm the set of democratic principles adopted at the last convention to guide DSA members when these issues arise within existing and future unions which include: 1. The right of members to vote on all collective bargaining agreements 2. All members to receive a copy of the CBA; prior to any contract vote, a complete copy (not just “highlights”) of proposed changes to the CBA will be available to all members, with time to review 3. Bargaining committees to include rank and file members 4. Direct election of officers at all levels – local and national 5. Officer salaries should be set close to that of the people they represent 6. Meetings, CBAs, constitutions, etc, to be translated (or conducted) into the languages spoken by 5% of members 7. Supporting Campaign Developing for Non-Reformist Labor Reforms Workers organizing on the shopfloor are already attempting to change and use the power of the state on the state and local level to scale organizing campaigns. Non-reformist labor reforms, such as sectoral bargaining, create openings for workers to organize and pave the way for more revolutionary change, by - for example - increasing workers power to directly confront the boss and/or creating new material conditions for workers to come together. To help chapters and organizing workers develop non-reformist reform campaigns, the Non-Reformist Reform Subcommittee of the NLC shall be created. The Subcommittee shall provide toolkits, training, cross-chapter coordination, and other campaign resources. This Subcommittee shall work with the NEC to coordinate with candidates and socialists-in-office around non-reformist reform positions and reform opportunities. 8. Growing and expanding NLC organizing projects and campaigns Going into the 2025-2027 term the NLC as outlined above will continue to build upon our success of the past. The fight for socialism means our projects such as EWOC, WOW, and the solidarity captain network must grow. This requires commitment, time, and people power. These projects will only be successful if we build capacity for them. In order to meet the moment and build power through these projects we must organize ourselves. The NLC through the work of its Membership Committee will focus on engaging rank-and-file DSA members in our nationwide projects. We further reaffirm the decision, made by the 2023 DSA Convention, that the NLC Co-chairs must be paid positions so that these political leaders have the capacity to do this vital work. Additionally, the NLC will establish a new regular Labor section in Democratic Left, which will principally be populated by reports from NLC campaigns, industrial sections, and chapter-level labor formations in our organization, in addition to hosting broader debates on labor strategy and tactics. Building robust internal infrastructures, such as but not limited to, an on-boarding process, shared discussion spaces, a collective calendar, and other resources are vital in building capacity for our work. *** Therefore be it resolved that DSA members will organize in their unions with their coworkers to support DSA-endorsed candidates and campaigns around winnable local issues connected to the following broad issues: 1. Medicare for All, 2. Bring Down the Cost of Living, 3. End Political Corruption, 4. Unions for All, and 5. End U.S. Militarism.

Therefore be it resolved that the NPC will work with the NLC and the NEC to identify in priority geographical areas: * unions with high densities of DSA members, * unions that have historically taken progressive political positions, * unions that are actively engaged in mass-participation organizing. * unions that have engaged in bargaining for the common good, * unions with upcoming contract expirations, * unions that have donated money to DSA-endorsed candidates, * unions that have run members for office, and develop training materials to help DSA members organize in their unions around candidate endorsements and winnable local issues. *** Therefore be it resolved that DSA chapters are encouraged to prioritize organizing with federal workers in support of the public services they provide to fight back against their bosses and our oligarchic political system; and

Be it further resolved that the NLC will create materials to support local chapters in carrying out activities including: * Bolstering federal worker contingents at the many large anti-Trump protests * Bringing together the federal workers already in our chapters * Hosting organizing trainings for the many federal workers ready to take action * Flyering outside federal buildings alongside federal workers * Holding mass meetings on the political moment and developments in the federal worker fight * Encouraging and joining informational pickets * Supporting federal union recruitment efforts such as e-dues conversion phonebanks and new organizing drives via volunteering with EWOC Capacity Commitment & Financial Impact Scores Capacity 4: High Finances 4: Greater than $50,000 This resolution commits significant financial and staffing resources to a multi-year national labor strategy culminating in a major mobilization around May Day 2028 . It includes hiring two full-time NLC Co-Chairs and expanding key labor programs like EWOC, WOW, and the Solidarity Fund. These efforts require substantial ongoing staff coordination and active participation from chapters and members nationwide. While the resolution does not specify exact figures beyond the salary of NLC co-chairs ($119.7k per full time employee per year), the scope of work indicates a high time commitment and significant financial investment. Status: Rejected Summary The authors of this amendment to the NLC Consensus Resolution wanted to put forward a partyist vision for the NLC. We believe only an independent socialist party can provide the basis for an independent labor movement, establishing practical links among the rank-and-file both in and between workplaces and coordinating our actions between the economic and political spheres. The following presents practical changes to inform the NLC Consensus Resolution towards this direction. Full text WHEREAS, workers unite into trade unions in order to win material concessions in the workplace, including improvements to wages and working conditions, as well as dignity and control over our lives. WHEREAS, under capitalism, no reform or concession can be durably won if not defended and expanded upon by revolutionary methods and class struggle. WHEREAS, unions are institutions which are meant to express the interests of workers in opposition to the interests of against capital. WHEREAS, the ultimate task of socialists organizing in the trade unions is to win the working class to the cause of socialism. WHEREAS, the US has a long history of labor leaders accepting business unionism, “plain and simple unionism”, or “free trade” unionism which utilize undemocratic methods to maintain cooperative relations with capitalist interests. WHEREAS, the labor movement and its leaders tend towards economism, an ideology that sacrifices the political struggle for full working class liberation in exchange for temporary economic gains for small sections of workers. WHEREAS, economism disengages and disempowers workers, and explicit political struggle brings more energy into the labor movement. WHEREAS, with the election of Trump, immigrants, women, queer and trans people, and workers in the US and around the world are under increased attack, and the labor movement has a key role to play in the struggle against the right wing and the capitalist system, a role it will only be able to fulfill through its politicization, democratization, and increased militancy. WHEREAS, DSA has a key role to play in promoting robust democratic reforms, developing the political activity of the rank and file, and spearheading the opposition to the oppression and exploitation of all working and oppressed peoples. WHEREAS, although reform movements in unions like the UAW and the Teamsters have won union leadership elections and have succeeded in implementing crucial democratic reforms within their unions, serious fractures have opened up within these movements over how to win political power for the working class. In the absence of a clear political alternative, leadership in these movements has largely continued the discredited strategy of supporting Democrats and even Republicans in exchange for short-term political favors for their individual sectors, at the cost of the labor movement’s political independence, and cross-sector and international solidarity between workers. WHEREAS, only an independent socialist party can provide the basis for an independent labor movement, establishing practical links among the rank-and-file both in and between workplaces and coordinating our actions between the economic and political spheres–between our labor organizers’ attacks on workplace dictatorship and our elected officials’ attacks on the authoritarian power of the owning class and undemocratic labor law, and between the working class of this country and the working class internationally. Be it therefore resolved, that CR10: NLC Consensus Resolution is amended as follows, with added text green and underlined, text removed red and struck out, and omitted text unaffected. [...] THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that this convention commits to continue its work of uniting the socialist and labor movements by committing DSA to a partyist labor strategy—that is, a strategy for strengthening the party coordination of DSA members in the labor movement—with the near term goal of turning May Day 2028 into a demonstration of bottom up worker power. [...] 1. Leading With Politics Two political strategies currently predominate among socialists in the labor movement: a sectarian approach, where socialists engage in agitation as part of a permanent campaign of pure opposition within their unions, and a economistic approach, where socialists tend to avoid raising socialist politics in the labor movement, instead deferring uncritically to reformist leaders. However, neither of these strategies offers a real solution to the crisis of political leadership in the labor movement. In pursuit of DSA’s wider goal of securing working class political independence, the NLC will lead and coordinate DSA members in the labor movement to organize against the Democratic Party, against the Republican Party and the authoritarian right wing, and for socialist politics. To build the socialist wing of the labor movement, the NLC will also coordinate the mass recruitment of union members into DSA. DSA members in the labor movement should always lead by example in our fights against workplace dictatorship and business unionism, and should take every opportunity to connect workplace struggles and union reform movements to the class struggle in general—to tenant struggles and housing justice, to the fight for universal healthcare, to the fight to extend suffrage and other democratic rights, to anti-imperialist solidarity and struggles for national self-determination, and ultimately a new democratic socialist society. 12. The primary task of industrial sections will be building union organization at the grassroots level through, for example, rank-and-file organization, shop steward networks, and activating union and labor-management committees. Industrial sections will also assist in running campaigns for union office or supporting democratic reformers. As more unions struggle with internal democracy, socialists must help build democratic structures to keep the union and its leadership accountable to its members, even when leadership is aligned with reform caucuses. The right of members to vote on all collective bargaining agreements The right of members to have democratic control of collective bargaining and the strategy around it. This strategy would include: 1. members electing democratic bargaining committees 2. members being consistently informed about the bargaining process 3. members having democratic discussions on the content of proposed agreements and decision making power over them 4. members being able to organize workplace actions, before, during and after negotiations 5. membership vote on all collective bargaining agreements 2. All members to receive a copy of the CBA; prior to any contract vote, a complete copy (not just “highlights”) of proposed changes to the CBA will be available to all members, with time to review 3. Bargaining committees to include rank and file members 4. Direct election of officers at all levels – local and national 5. Officer salaries should be set close to that of the people they represent 6. Meetings, CBAs, constitutions, etc, to be translated (or conducted) into the languages spoken by 5% of members 7. Functioning shop floor democracy that includes regular meetings of shop stewards/representatives of the members. 8. The right of members to control the political endorsements of their unions 9. Regular, open and deliberative meetings of the general membership following agreed-upon rules of order 78. Status: Referred to NPC Summary This resolution outlines several improvements to DSA’s growth and development and national-chapter coordination, including monthly national talking points/messaging guidelines, expanded monthly members’ bulletins, bi-monthly national membership forums, a chapter training program, and intentional new chapter development efforts. Full text Whereas, our growth and development strategy must be rooted in an analysis of the political conditions and include political priorities to be effective. Whereas, DSA is organizing in explosive terrain. Protest movements are erupting in opposition to Donald Trump and the membership of DSA is growing rapidly. Whereas, a member-driven, campaigning approach is the most effective way to grow DSA. Whereas, DSA presently grows almost entirely through passive recruitment without an organized and consistently applied national strategy. Therefore, be it resolved, to provide a strong political lead to DSA, the convention tasks the NPC with creating monthly “talking points” guidelines. These guidelines will be a short political analysis which speaks on the essential aspects of major current events, and how chapters are recommended to talk about them. The GDC will be tasked with distributing these talking points to chapters, and working with the Communications Committee to create template graphics and posts about them. These talking points should be distributed in regular members’ bulletins. Therefore be it resolved, to provide clear information and resources to members, and assure accountable, democratic and public discussion about growth and development, the NPC and Communications Committee is tasked with publishing expanded monthly bulletins, distributed to all members, that contain, in addition to existing information, the following points: * Short updates from DSA committees. * Short updates from our 10 largest chapters and other chapters the NPC chooses to highlight. * Data with membership numbers, the fastest growing chapters, and progress on any dues, membership and fundraising drives. * Brief political analysis/talking points from the NPC on major current events. * A schedule of major upcoming DSA events. * A link for committee applications. * These bulletins will be emailed to all members and posted on our discussion board. Therefore be it resolved, to ensure a regular process of discussion, engagement and feedback to the members, the NPC, NPEC and GDC are tasked with holding a membership forum, open to the whole membership, to discuss a major event, reflect on a campaign, or debate questions of theory or analysis, at least every two months. Such forums should provide at least 30 minutes for members to ask questions or make comments or arguments. The NPC is empowered to decide which format of these forums is the most useful at the time, whether that be a debate, interview, open discussion, a training, or a panel discussion. Therefore be it resolved, to develop a strong culture of politicized interventions in DSA the GDC will be tasked with holding training sessions for chapters. At these trainings, chapters will learn the following points: * Chapters will learn tabling strategy and be encouraged to engage in weekly tabling * Chapters will learn how to do listwork * Chapters will learn how to develop an internal recruitment and membership development pipeline * Chapters will learn how to have organizing conversations * Chapters will learn how to run & plan strategic campaigns * Chapters will learn how to create chapter materials such as pamphlets and flyers Therefore be it resolved, to establish new chapters and advance the growth of DSA, the GDC is tasked with reaching out one on one to DSA members in significant population areas that do not currently have a chapter, and working with them to establish an organizing committee.
